Athymic mice and Rag1 -/- mice with preserved thymic stroma are comparably resistant to PMOS-like pathology, supporting an essential role for thymus-derived T cells in disease development. Antibody-mediated depletion further reveals CD8 + , but not CD4 + , T cells are required for disease manifestation. Among CD8 + T-cell subsets, virtual memory CD8 + T (T VM ) cells preferentially expand in patients and experimental models and accumulate in reproductive tissues. These cells exacerbate disease severity and prolong pathology after androgen withdrawal. Mechanistically, ovarian T VM cells secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines and CCL5, thereby recruiting myeloid cells to the ovary and amplifying local inflammation. Therapeutically, JAK inhibition restricts T VM -cell differentiation, redirects CD8 + T-cell fate away from a cytotoxic CXCR3 high state and ameliorates PMOS-like pathology. These findings identify T VM cells as key effectors linking androgen-induced thymic remodeling to ovarian inflammation and persistent pathology.

papers.title: Behaviorally-relevant features of observed actions dominate cortical representational geometry in natural vision.
papers.abstract: We effortlessly extract behaviorally relevant information from dynamic visual input to understand the actions of others. Here, we compare behavioral judgments of action meaning against other models capturing semantic and visual features. We measured brain activity using fMRI while participants viewed 90 video clips depicting social and nonsocial actions in real-world contexts. Using arrangement tasks, we developed two behavioral models capturing judgments of action meaning (transitive purpose, social content), as well as three control models capturing judgments of visual content (people, objects, scene). We compared these models with semantic models based on word embeddings and visual models based on gaze and motion energy. Behavioral models of action meaning outperformed models of visual content, semantics, and low-level visual features across much of cortex. Transitivity and sociality captured large portions of unique variance throughout the action observation network, extending into regions not typically associated with action perception, such as ventral temporal cortex.

papers.title: The brain of the female Anopheles gambiae mosquito at spatial and single-cell resolution.
papers.abstract: Blood feeding in Anopheles mosquitoes is at the root of all malaria infections in humans and is supported by a range of physiological and behavioral adaptations. Since behavior is orchestrated at the level of the central nervous system, we surveyed the cellular diversity and spatial organization of the female Anopheles gambiae brain and compared it to other insect species. We then describe transcriptional changes associated with mosquito life history events with single brain and single-cell RNA sequencing. We did not identify expansion of specific cell populations, but a modulation of neurotransmission in the mated mosquitoes, and a metabolic and immune response associated with glia, Kenyon cells and immune cells after bloodmeal, and detected signatures of aging in the mosquito brain. We did not find an effect of Plasmodium falciparum infection. Our atlas will empower the study of non-model insect neurobiology, neural basis of vector behavior, and mechanisms underlying malaria transmission.

papers.title: Compartmentalized coenzyme A and ferroptosis vulnerability in PKAN and CoPAN.
papers.abstract: Ferroptotic vulnerability may arise from the failure of a local antioxidant defense even when whole-cell metabolite abundance appears preserved. Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) and COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration (CoPAN), two forms of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation caused by defects in coenzyme A (CoA) synthesis, provide a genetically defined setting for examining this possibility. We propose that impairment of the mitochondrial CoA pool can weaken a CoA-dependent redox defense without requiring a measurable whole-cell CoA deficit, while regional iron burden and oxidative demand lower the threshold for ferroptotic death. This model could reconcile apparently preserved bulk CoA with selective neuronal vulnerability. It is testable, remains to be validated directly in patient-derived models, and distinguishes mitochondrial CoA availability from total cellular CoA as the disease-relevant variable.

papers.title: Low-intensity focused ultrasound for neuromodulation: neuroimaging and neurointerventional perspectives.
papers.abstract: Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is an emerging, noninvasive neuromodulation technique with a growing evidence base and set of applications. LIFU uses low-energy acoustic waves that are focused to a focal volume in the millimeter range and transiently modulate neuronal activity in targeted cortical and subcortical brain structures. Unlike high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), which is designed to cause thermal ablation of the target tissue, LIFU is intended to modulate neuronal activity rather than ablate tissue. In this article, we review the technical background, clinical applications, and safety of LIFU from neuroimaging and neurointerventional perspectives.

papers.title: Effects of Different Exercise Modalities on Interleukin-6, Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor, and Cognitive Function in Obese Older Women.
papers.abstract: This study examined the effects of different exercise modalities on body composition, interleukin-6 (IL-6), and cognitive function in obese older women. A total of 54 women aged ≥65 years were randomized to the control (CON), aerobic aquatic exercise (AAE), aerobic dance exercise (ADE), or combined aerobic and resistance exercise (AE+RE) groups. Significant time-by-group interactions were observed for body weight (BW), body fat percentage (%BF), IL-6, and Korean version of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE-K) scores. The AAE and ADE groups showed significant reductions in BW and %BF, and fat-free mass increased only in the AAE group ( P <0.01). brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) increased in the AAE and ADE groups (both P <0.01), whereas IL-6 decreased in both groups (ADE, P <0.05; AAE, P <0.01). MMSE-K scores improved in all exercise groups, with scores in the AE+RE and AAE groups significantly higher than those in the CON group ( P <0.001 and P <0.01, respectively). Moderate-intensity aquatic and dance-based aerobic exercise over 12 weeks improved both metabolic health and cognitive function in obese older women and was accompanied by reductions in IL-6 and increases in BDNF.

papers.title: Insulin regulates activity-dependent mitochondrial depolarization and calcium dynamics in dentate granule cells.
papers.abstract: Systemic insulin resistance is associated with reduced hippocampal energy metabolism and cognitive impairment both in humans and animal models. However, whether insulin rapidly regulates neuronal metabolic stability during activity remains unclear. Here, we examined insulin signaling and queried the corresponding mitochondrial responses in dentate granule cells (DGCs) of adult female mice. This layer of excitatory neurons within the hippocampus plays an essential role in learning and memory. Insulin robustly increased Akt phosphorylation in dentate gyrus tissue when insulin degradation was inhibited, and this response was attenuated by genetic deletion of the insulin receptor in DGCs, consistent with cell-autonomous signaling. We found that insulin did not alter mitochondrial membrane potential at rest, but significantly limited activity-evoked mitochondrial depolarization induced by neuronal stimulation. However, this change had no measurable impact on cytosolic ATP availability and was instead associated with Ca 2+ dynamics. Removing Ca 2+ ions from the extracellular solution, or disrupting mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake, prevented insulin modulation of the mitochondrial membrane potential. Furthermore, insulin limited cytosolic Ca 2+ accumulation through an insulin receptor-dependent mechanism that persisted despite Akt inhibition. Insulin also accelerated the clearance of mitochondrial Ca 2+ transients in active neurons, which occurred without changes in either neuronal excitability or pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphorylation. Together, these findings identify endogenous insulin degradation as a key regulator of hippocampal insulin signaling, and reveal a previously unrecognized interaction between insulin and Ca 2+ signaling in stimulated DGCs. This work also establishes a direct link between central insulin signaling and the maintenance of mitochondrial electrochemical homeostasis in the adult brain. Significance Statement Insulin signaling is known to influence synaptic plasticity, yet its direct effects on neuronal metabolism remain poorly defined. Here, we show that endogenous insulin degradation limits insulin signaling in adult hippocampal tissue. This finding suggests that inhibitors of the insulin degrading enzyme may hold the potential to improve the efficacy of insulin-based interventions aimed at improving learning and memory. Acute insulin signaling does not modify neuronal excitability, or cytosolic ATP availability. Instead, it stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces calcium accumulation in active dentate granule cells. By identifying an insulin-dependent mechanism that regulates the electrochemical homeostasis of mitochondria in active neurons, this work provides insight into how brain insulin resistance may contribute to cognitive dysfunction in aging and neurometabolic disorders.

papers.title: A pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts hippocampal synapse maturation and homeostasis.
papers.abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for activity-dependent synapse maturation and circuit development. De novo missense mutations in AMPAR subunits are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet how these variants disrupt neuronal function remains unclear. Here, we examine a recurrent pathogenic mutation in the GluA1 subunit (GRIA1 p.A636T) that alters AMPAR function and is associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using GluA1 A636T knock-in mice of either sex, we identify impairments in hippocampal-dependent learning and working memory. Quantitative proteomics combined with bulk RNA-seq revealed age-dependent molecular remodeling in mutant hippocampus. Synaptic protein alterations were present in juvenile and adult mice, whereas a pronounced upregulation of mitochondrial and glial-associated proteins emerged more strongly in adulthood. Transcriptomic analyses showed partial concordance and highlighted divergence between RNA and protein regulation. Consistent with these molecular changes, there were increases in markers of oxidative stress in juvenile and adult mutant animals, whereas altered mitochondria morphology emerged selectively in adult mutants. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated reduced basal excitatory transmission, persistence of silent synapses in adulthood and exaggerated activity-dependent synaptic potentiation, which were associated with reduced spine size consistent with impaired synapse maturation. Together, these findings indicate that a pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts developmental synapse maturation with secondary metabolic adaptations emerging over time. Significance Statement Mutations in genes encoding AMPA-type glutamate receptors are increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism and intellectual disability. However, how these mutations disrupt brain function and development remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model carrying a recurrent disease-associated mutation in the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit, we show that the presence of this mutant subunit protein impairs the normal maturation of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus. Mutant mice retain immature "silent" synapses into adulthood, exhibit abnormal synaptic plasticity, reduced spine size, and deficits in learning and memory. Molecular analyses reveal age-dependent remodeling of synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, suggesting that metabolic changes arise secondary to disrupted synapse development. These findings clarify how pathogenic AMPA receptor variants alter brain function over time.

papers.title: Endpoint-specific interactions between aerobic exercise and benfotiamine in chronic noise-induced prefrontal cortical dysfunction in mice.
papers.abstract: Chronic environmental noise can impair brain redox and inflammatory homeostasis, but the effects of combined non-pharmacological and metabolic interventions remain unclear. This study investigated whether aerobic exercise and benfotiamine, separately or combined, attenuate noise-induced behavioral dysfunction and prefrontal cortical injury-related changes. Male Swiss albino mice were assigned to Control, Noise, Noise + aerobic exercise, Noise + benfotiamine (200 mg/kg/day), Noise + aerobic exercise + benfotiamine, or Noise + N-acetylcysteine (500 mg/kg/day) groups (n = 9/group). Noise-exposed mice received broadband industrial noise at 90 dB sound pressure level for 4 h/day for 28 days. Behavioral despair-like phenotypes, cortical redox status, inflammatory gene expression, and histopathology were evaluated. Noise increased immobility in the forced swim and tail suspension tests, elevated reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, malondialdehyde, protein carbonyls, and pro-inflammatory transcripts, and reduced glutathione and antioxidant capacity. Both interventions attenuated multiple abnormalities. Aerobic exercise produced prominent behavioral effects and increased interleukin-10 expression, whereas benfotiamine strongly reduced reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation, and interleukin-1β. Significant exercise × benfotiamine interactions occurred for both behavioral tests, reactive oxygen species, tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-10, but not for several other endpoints. The combined intervention frequently produced the most favorable absolute values, although significant interactions were generally subadditive rather than synergistic. Aerobic exercise and benfotiamine therefore provide broad but endpoint-specific protection against chronic noise-associated prefrontal cortical dysfunction.

papers.title: Exploratory chromosome 14-focused transcriptomic profiling of PSEN1-associated familial Alzheimer's disease across brain regions.
papers.abstract: Familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD) is an inherited form of early-onset Alzheimer's disease associated with pathogenic variants in presenilin 1 (PSEN1). To explore chromosome 14-associated transcriptional patterns in FAD across anatomically distinct brain regions, publicly available RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) datasets from frontal cortex, temporal cortex, and whole-brain samples were analyzed. Because one FAD sample and one control sample were available for each brain region, expression differences were evaluated descriptively using observed log₂ fold-change values rather than conventional inferential differential-expression statistics. Functional annotation and protein-protein interaction analyses were subsequently used to provide biological context for the observed expression patterns. Distinct regional expression patterns were observed within the chromosome 14-focused dataset. Higher expression was observed for representative genes including FITM1, IFI27, AHSA1, and NFKBIA in the frontal cortex, and DHRS4L2, ESR2, GPR65, EFCAB11, and HOMEZ in the temporal cortex. The observed expression patterns were associated with inflammatory, cellular stress, metabolic, receptor-mediated, proteostatic, and neuronal signaling-related functions. Network analysis was used to contextualize these expression patterns rather than to infer causal regulatory relationships. Five representative proteins-NFKBIA, ESR2, GPR65, AHSA1, and IFI27-were further examined structural information to provide structural context for selected transcriptomic observations. Given the absence of biological replication and the chromosome 14-focused design, these findings should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Independent replicated cohorts and complementary transcriptomic, proteomic, and functional studies are required to determine the reproducibility and biological relevance of the observed patterns.

papers.title: Unraveling gut-brain crosstalk: Lessons from Drosophila and other insect models.
papers.abstract: Bidirectional communication between the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system is emerging as a fundamental regulatory principle across animal phyla. Insects, the model organism Drosophila melanogaster in particular, have become powerful models for dissecting this crosstalk at cellular and molecular resolution. Recent advances reveal conserved enteroendocrine neuropeptide signaling pathways and neuronal circuits that regulate feeding behavior, metabolism, and physiological homeostasis. Here we review progress over the past decade, highlight mechanistic insights that are broadly relevant to mammalian biology, and discuss open questions that insect models are positioned to address.

papers.title: CircPDS5B knockdown attenuates sevoflurane-induced developmental neurotoxicity and associated intracellular alkalinization.
papers.abstract: Neonatal sevoflurane exposure can cause developmental neurotoxicity, but the molecular events linking anesthetic exposure to neuronal injury remain incompletely understood. We examined whether circPDS5B-associated disruption of intracellular acid-base homeostasis contributes to this injury. Primary hippocampal neurons and postnatal day 5 (P5) rats were exposed to 4.0% sevoflurane for 6 h. Cultured neurons were transduced with adenovirus on day 4 in vitro (DIV 4), and neonatal rats received bilateral microinjections of Ad-sh-circPDS5B into hippocampal CA1 at P3. In vitro, sevoflurane increased circPDS5B expression, reduced miR-92a-3p and carbonic anhydrase IX (CA9) levels, and induced intracellular alkalinization, reduced viability, and organelle ultrastructural abnormalities. Dual-luciferase assays supported a sequence-specific interaction between circPDS5B and miR-92a-3p. CircPDS5B knockdown increased miR-92a-3p and CA9 expression toward control levels, attenuated intracellular alkalinization, and was associated with less prominent mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum ultrastructural abnormalities. In vivo, circPDS5B knockdown attenuated the sevoflurane-associated reductions in hippocampal CA9 expression and CA1 dendritic spine density and was associated with improved subsequent behavioral performance in the Morris water maze and open-field test. These findings support an association between circPDS5B dysregulation, altered intracellular pH regulation, and sevoflurane-induced developmental neurotoxicity. The circPDS5B/miR-92a-3p/CA9 axis should be considered a candidate regulatory mechanism pending pathway-specific rescue experiments.

papers.title: Role and mechanism of ATF6-mediated endoplasmic reticulum stress in ITLN-1 against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury.
papers.abstract: Intelectin-1 (ITLN-1), a novel adipocytokine, exerts neuroprotective effects against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI), yet its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study focused on activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6), a key endoplasmic reticulum stress sensor, to explore its role in CIRI-induced neuronal injury and determine whether ITLN-1 mediates neuroprotection through ATF6 regulation. We established an N2a cell hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) model and a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model. Using protein molecular docking, situ proximity ligation assay, Western blotting, mitochondrial membrane potential assays, and TUNEL staining, we investigated ATF6 activation in neuronal apoptosis and its upstream regulatory mechanisms. H/R injury markedly induced ATF6 activation in N2a cells, triggering mitochondrial dysfunction and promoting apoptosis. ATF6 overexpression further aggravated these effects, confirming its critical pathogenic role in CIRI. Mechanistic analyses revealed that ITLN-1 physically associates with ATF6. Both ITLN-1 overexpression and exogenous recombinant ITLN-1 administration significantly suppressed excessive ATF6 activation, modulated the JNK signaling pathway, improved cell viability, reduced intracellular calcium overload and reactive oxygen species accumulation, and attenuated neuronal apoptosis. In vivo, ITLN-1 ameliorated neurological deficits, reduced neuronal damage, and alleviated demyelination, whereas ITLN-1 knockdown produced opposite effects. Excessive ATF6 activation underlies CIRI-induced neuronal injury. ITLN-1 exerts neuroprotection by inhibiting ATF6 and modulating JNK signaling, thereby alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction and reducing apoptosis. These findings highlight the ITLN-1/ATF6 axis as a promising therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

papers.title: Essential Oils From the Fruit of Amomum villosum Lour. Alleviate LPS-Induced Neuroinflammation by Repressing PI3K-Akt and MAPK Signaling Pathways.
papers.abstract: Amomum villosum Lour. has been traditionally valued in various cultures for its health benefits. Here, we show that the neuroprotective effects of the essential oils extracted from the fruit of Amomum villosum Lour. (AVEO) and elucidate its underlying mechanisms in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced neuroinflammation. The main compounds of AVEO can cross the blood-brain barrier and significantly improve cognitive and behavioral dysfunction in LPS-induced mice, leading to a 50% enhancement in Morris water maze performance, a 60% and 80% reduction in immobility time in the tail suspension test and forced swimming test, respectively. Moreover, AVEO mitigates neuron loss and suppresses the expression of pro-inflammatory mediators, including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, while upregulating the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 in brain tissue. RNA-seq and metabonomics analyses reveal that AVEO modulates multiple inflammation-related pathways and restore metabolic homeostasis in brain tissue. Remarkably, AVEO attenuates hyperactivation of the PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling pathways in LPS-induced microglia and improves neuronal damage in LPS-induced microglia-neuron co-culture system. Altogether, our findings suggest that AVEO alleviates neural dysfunction by modulating PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling cascades and promoting metabolic reprogramming upon neuroinflammation, thereby revealing the therapeutic potential of AVEO in several neurological disorders.

papers.title: Sustained induction of PMOS-like phenotype in mice exposed to letrozole in drinking water.
papers.abstract: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS; formerly polycystic ovary syndrome) is the most common endocrinopathy affecting women of reproductive age, characterized by ovarian dysfunction and hyperandrogenism, with metabolic disturbances including insulin resistance and obesity also present for 50% of PMOS patients. Effective preclinical models are crucial for evaluating therapeutic interventions. However, current mouse models of hyperandrogenemia induced by aromatase inhibition typically rely on subcutaneous letrozole implants, which require surgical procedures and struggle to sustain PMOS-like phenotypes over an extended period necessary for thorough drug assessment. We hypothesized that an oral letrozole administration would provide extended maintenance of syndrome-like features. Female mice received letrozole either via subcutaneous implant (~1.67 mg/kg/day for 70 days) or orally in drinking water (~1 mg/kg/day for up to 130 days). Estrous cyclicity was monitored by vaginal cytology. Hormonal, metabolic, and histological assessments were performed. While a subcutaneous letrozole implant only sustained hyperandrogenic, metabolic and reproductive phenotypes for ~50 days, oral letrozole administration sustained complete anovulation for at least 100 days, maintaining a persistent diestrus stage. The oral letrozole treatment produced comprehensive PMOS-like features, including significantly elevated testosterone levels, increased luteinizing hormone concentration, pulse frequency and amplitude, enhanced hypothalamic androgen receptor expression, decreased hypothalamic progesterone receptor expression, cystic-like ovarian morphology, increased body weight, impaired insulin sensitivity, and elevated adiposity during the entire time of the treatment period (18 weeks), compared to the placebo treatment. Uterine weight was not decreased, suggesting normal circulating estrogen concentrations. These findings demonstrate that oral letrozole delivery offers a more accessible method of administration, resulting in a sustained induction of PMOS-like phenotypes. This approach effectively maintains both reproductive and metabolic features essential for comprehensive evaluation, thereby enhancing the model's utility for investigating therapeutic interventions in PMOS.

papers.title: DA-S 2 RL: Disease-aware shared-specific representation learning for heterogeneous image-EHR Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Combining electronic health records (EHR) with medical images is important for improving the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, neuroimages and EHR differ greatly in semantic content and data distribution. Neuroimages mainly reflect brain structure and metabolic abnormalities, while EHR records clinical symptoms and behavioral changes. Directly fusing these heterogeneous modalities may mix shared disease information with modality-specific diagnostic cues, resulting in redundant and ambiguous representations. To address this problem, we propose DA-S 2 RL, a disease-aware shared-specific multimodal representation learning framework for AD diagnosis. DA-S 2 RL organizes heterogeneous image and EHR features into disease-related shared semantics and modality-specific diagnostic residuals. The core of DA-S 2 RL is the shared-specific cross-modal coding (SCC) module. It strengthens cross-modal semantic consistency, suppresses redundant correlations, and enables mutual refinement between shared semantics and diagnostic residuals. Before SCC, image features are integrated into a compact image representation, and EHR features are encoded into the same feature space. Experiments on ADNI and NACC demonstrate that explicitly organizing heterogeneous image-EHR representations into shared disease semantics and modality-specific residuals improves multimodal diagnostic learning under different image-EHR settings.

papers.title: Reduced perivascular diffusion in multiple sclerosis is associated with aging, disease duration, and mobility impairment.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system supports brain homeostasis by facilitating perivascular fluid transport and metabolic waste clearance. Diffusion-tensor imaging along the perivascular space (ALPS-index) provides a non-invasive surrogate marker of glymphatic activity. The objectives of this study were to: (1) compare the ALPS-index between individuals with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) and non-MS controls, (2) examine the role of age in the association between ALPS-index and disease duration, and (3) examine the relationship between ALPS-index and walking speed in RRMS. Individuals with RRMS and age‑ and sex-matched controls underwent 3T MRI, including diffusion‑weighted imaging. ALPS‑index was calculated using standardized regions of interest. Walking function was assessed using a two‑minute walk test. Individuals with RRMS have significantly lower ALPS‑index compared to controls (p = 0.001). Across participants, older age was associated with lower ALPS‑index (p < 0.001), with no evidence that age effects differed by group (group effect: p = 0.311, group x age: p = 0.954). In RRMS, a lower ALPS‑index was associated with longer disease duration (p = 0.028); however, mediation analyses showed that chronological age largely explained this relationship (p = 0.012). In a multivariable model, both lower ALPS‑index and slower gait speed were independently associated with longer disease duration, with an interaction effect (p = 0.032) suggesting functional compensation between perivascular diffusion and mobility. These findings highlight the interconnected roles of aging, perivascular fluid transport, and mobility in MS and support the ALPS‑index as a feasible, non‑invasive imaging marker of age‑related vulnerability.

papers.title: Intranasal Delivery of an Antioxidant Nanoassembly for Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury via Drd2/β-arrestin2/ERK Signaling.
papers.abstract: Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) is caused by reduced cerebral blood flow, leading to excessive oxidative stress and neurological deficits. Curcumin (Cur) is a promising therapeutic agent, but its antioxidant activity is limited by low bioavailability and poor brain penetration. Herein, an intranasal delivery strategy using a tetrahedral framework nucleic acid (tFNAs)-Cur nanoassembly (tFNAs-Cur) was employed for CIRI treatment. tFNAs-Cur was synthesized through self-assembly, achieving a high Cur loading efficiency of 87% and exhibiting potent scavenging activity against reactive oxygen species (ROS) including O2·-, ·OH, and H2O2. In vitro studies showed that tFNAs-Cur inhibited oxygen glucose deprivation/reoxygenation-induced ROS elevation of cytoplasm and mitochondria, and enhanced proliferation and migration of SH-SY5Y cells. In vivo studies demonstrated that intranasal administration of tFNAs-Cur reduced cerebral infarct volume, enhanced neuronal survival, and improved neurological and behavioral outcomes in middle cerebral artery occlusion rats. Further mechanistic investigation using RNA sequencing revealed that tFNAs-Cur exerted its effects by activating the Drd2/β-arrestin2/ERK signaling, thereby improving mitochondrial function and upregulating BDNF levels. Furthermore, hemolysis assays, serum biochemical measurements, and histopathological analyses demonstrated that tFNAs-Cur possessed a favorable biosafety profile both ex vivo and in vivo. This study provides an intranasal antioxidant nanoassembly strategy for CIRI and holds potential for clinical translation.

papers.title: Impact of setmelanotide on metabolic syndrome risk in patients with proopiomelanocortin or leptin receptor deficiencies.
papers.abstract: Patients with severe obesity due to proopiomelanocortin (POMC) or leptin receptor (LEPR) deficiencies resulting in impaired melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) signaling may be at risk for obesity-related comorbidities. Here, we report metabolic parameters and metabolic syndrome severity in patients before and after treatment with the MC4R agonist setmelanotide. Patients from phase 3 studies of setmelanotide for POMC (NCT02896192) or LEPR (NCT03287960) deficiencies with complete metabolic parameter data were included in this analysis. Metabolic parameters and metabolic severity Z scores based on body mass index (MetS-Z-BMI scores) were reported at baseline and following ∼1 year of setmelanotide treatment in these patients; subgroup analyses were conducted by sex, age, genotype, and response to treatment. Metabolic parameters were evaluated in 18 of 21 patients enrolled in phase 3 trials. Group means for most parameters were within the normal range at baseline, excluding weight-related measures, fasting glucose, and triglycerides. The overall baseline mean (standard deviation [SD]) MetS-Z-BMI score was 1.49 (1.33). Most patients saw improvement in ≥1 metabolic parameter at week 52. The overall mean (SD) change in MetS-Z-BMI score after ∼1 year of treatment was -1.05 (0.88). Among subgroup analyses, MetS-Z-BMI score reductions were significantly greater in achievers of weight-based thresholds compared with nonachievers (P = .0187) and in patients with deficiencies in POMC compared with LEPR (P = .0278). Setmelanotide was associated with a reduction in specific metabolic parameters and metabolic syndrome severity (MetS-Z-BMI scores) in patients with POMC or LEPR deficiencies.

papers.title: Evaluation of Methylmercury-Induced Motor Dysfunction and Proteomic Analysis of Cerebrospinal Fluid in Common Marmosets (Callithrix jacchus).
papers.abstract: Methylmercury (MeHg) poisoning can lead to Minamata disease, often manifesting as motor dysfunction. We aimed to establish a quantitative evaluation method for MeHg exposure-associated motor dysfunction in the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus). Three male marmosets were orally administered MeHg (1.5 mg Hg/kg/day) for 2 weeks, followed by a 2-week non-treatment period; three control marmosets received vehicle. Walking and spontaneous behavior were recorded weekly. After marking body segments, bounding gait videos were analyzed to assess locomotion speed, hip joint position, knee angle, dorsal neck-to-torso angle, and spontaneous behavior. In Hg-1 (MeHg-exposed marmoset with earliest symptom onset), locomotion speed and stride length decreased, while stride time increased. In Hg-2 (second marmoset to exhibit symptom onset), hip joint position and knee angle initially showed relatively normal fluctuations during bounding gait. However, their lower limits decreased following MeHg administration, and the dorsal neck-to-torso angle shifted from negative to positive. Spontaneous activity of Hg-1 and Hg-2 significantly decreased after MeHg administration. These results indicate that MeHg exposure-associated motor dysfunction in marmosets can be detected using our method, with particularly prominent lower-limb abnormalities. Furthermore, cerebrospinal fluid proteomic profiling revealed coordinated disruptions converging on three pathological axes-neuronal injury and neuroprotective responses, neuronal metabolic failure and cytosolic enzyme leakage, and impaired transport and homeostatic regulation-identifying nine proteins as candidate biomarkers. Proteomic alterations were consistent with the observed neuronal injury, neuroinflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and impaired homeostatic regulation in affected motor pathways. These findings establish the marmoset as a translational primate model for neurotoxicological assessments and biomarker discovery.

papers.title: Drosophila dendrites are resilient to adult-onset deficits in mitochondrial dynamics.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial transport, fusion, and fission are necessary for neuronal development, but the role of mitochondrial dynamics in neuronal maintenance remains unclear. In this work, we employed functional in vivo imaging of neurons in the Drosophila visual system, "horizontal system" (HS) cells, to determine how adult-onset deficits in mitochondrial dynamics affect mitochondrial localization, local regulation of ATP, and dendrite maintenance. In mature HS neurons, inhibition of mitochondrial transport or fusion depleted mitochondria from the dendrite over time but, surprisingly, had no effect on dendrite morphology. Moreover, adult-restricted mitochondrial mislocalization affected neither visual stimulus-driven dendritic calcium responses nor local, dynamic regulation of ATP levels. In contrast, when induced during development, the same perturbations caused mitochondrial mislocalization, loss of dendrite complexity, abrogation of stimulus-locked calcium responses and ATP fluctuations, and age-dependent dendrite degeneration. Thus, although mitochondrial dynamics are necessary during neuronal development, mature dendrites are capable of maintaining form and function in vivo upon mitochondrial depletion.

papers.title: Novel therapies for glioblastoma.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma is the most aggressive and treatment-resistant primary brain tumor in adults. Given its clinical severity and biological complexity, research efforts are focused on understanding and targeting intratumoral heterogeneity, adaptive resistance, drug delivery barriers, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. This review highlights emerging therapeutic approaches for the treatment of glioblastoma including advances in radiation planning, molecularly targeted therapy, immunotherapy, blood-brain barrier modulation, and neuronal signaling. Radiation therapy remains a cornerstone of glioblastoma treatment, and advances in image-guided planning are being developed to refine treatment margins and improve tolerability without compromising efficacy. Blood-brain barrier permeability is being improved through device-assisted approaches, including focused ultrasound in combination with systemic therapies. Molecularly targeted and immunotherapeutic approaches continue to be evaluated, increasingly with biomarker-informed strategies to optimize patient selection. In parallel, drug repurposing, neuronal modulation, and metabolic interventions have shown promising preclinical and retrospective signals and are moving towards prospective studies. Interventions to improve quality of life are also underway with early palliative care showing significant impact for patients with glioblastoma. As the field moves towards tailored and precision-guided approaches, combination strategies remain central to addressing the multiple mechanisms by which glioblastoma evades treatment.

papers.title: Biomarker-guided treatment strategies for patients with gliomas in clinical practice.
papers.abstract: Targeted therapy has made important contributions to improving outcomes for patients with many solid tumors, but has had only limited activity so far in patients with gliomas, notably glioblastoma. Failure of targeted therapy in glioblastoma is likely due to redundance of oncogenic pathway activation and so far the inability to identify suitable targets and apply biomarker-based enrichment strategies in clinical trial designs. In contrast, in non-glioblastoma tumors, there are promising developments which have already changed clinical practice: inhibition of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) exemplified by vorasidenib, the first approved drug specifically for IDH-mutant gliomas, has changed the landscape for targeted therapy of WHO grade 2 gliomas. Furthermore, dordaviprone, an antagonist of dopamine receptor D2/3 (DRD2/3) and an allosteric agonist of the mitochondrial protease caseinolytic mitochondrial matrix peptidase proteolytic subunit (ClpP), emerges as a potentially active agent in patients with recurrent K27M-mutant diffuse midline gliomas. Finally, BRAF mutations, neurotrophic tyrosine receptor kinase ( r fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) gene fusions continue to raise interest as therapeutic targets at least for subsets of patients with gliomas. Almost no targeted therapy approaches for ependymomas have emerged. Improved clinical trial designs including shared control arms early on and using pharmacodynamic endpoints ideally in enriched patient populations are the path forward towards the identification of further active treatments for patients with gliomas. Targeted therapy defines treatment strategies that are designed to interfere with a specific metabolic signaling pathway that maintains growth of a specific type of tumor. Among primary brain tumors, dependence of growth on one single signaling pathway is rare. This has limited the role of targeted therapy, notably in glioblastoma, the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults. In some brain tumors other than glioblastoma, there are promising developments which have already changed clinical practice, notably inhibition of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) in tumors with IDH mutations. Novel targets are currently being explored in various types of rare brain tumors.

papers.title: Severe Hypoxic-ischaemic Encephalopathy and Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy Following Accidental Butane Exposure: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Butane is a highly lipophilic aliphatic hydrocarbon widely used as a domestic fuel and aerosol propellant. Acute exposure in enclosed environments may cause severe neurological and cardiovascular toxicity through oxygen displacement, respiratory depression, myocardial sensitisation to catecholamines, and potentially direct toxic effects. A 45-year-old woman was found unconscious in a small, closed studio apartment, while her husband was found deceased in the same environment. Subsequent inspection by the judicial authorities identified deterioration of the gas tubing associated with a gas leak. The patient presented in deep coma (Glasgow Coma Scale score 5) and required tracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Initial carboxyhaemoglobin was 16.9% and progressively normalised during oxygen therapy. Brain imaging demonstrated extensive cortical, deep grey matter, brainstem, cerebellar, and white-matter abnormalities consistent with severe hypoxic-ischaemic injury. Cardiac evaluation showed mild ST-segment elevation, increased cardiac biomarkers, and severe transient Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction (LVEF 25%) with a pattern highly suggestive of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy; LVEF subsequently improved to 44%. Severe neurological impairment persisted, and the patient was transferred to neurological rehabilitation. She died approximately six months after the index event; reliable documentation of the precise cause of death was unavailable. This case illustrates the severe neurological and cardiovascular consequences that may follow accidental butane exposure in an enclosed environment. The coexistence of extensive hypoxic- ischaemic brain injury and transient stress-related ventricular dysfunction highlights the importance of integrated neurological, cardiological, and toxicological assessment.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evaluation of Psilocybin in Neurodegenerative Disorders: Relevance of 5-HT2A Receptors and Downstream Pathways.
papers.abstract: More than fifty million individuals worldwide are experiencing neurodegenerative disorders, which include Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, multiple sclerosis, and frontotemporal dementia. These disorders have a significant role in the gradual degradation of cognition and motor skills. Most current treatment approaches have little effect on changing the course of the disease and are largely symptomatic. Psilocybin, a naturally occurring tryptamine alkaloid from psilocybin mushrooms, has become a promising medicinal agent because of its hallucinogenic, neuroprotective, and neuroplastic properties. After being metabolically transformed into its active form, psilocin, it primarily activates serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. This modulates glutamatergic neurotransmission and neurotrophic signaling pathways such as BDNF/TrkB and mTOR, which regulate synaptic remodeling, dendritic complexity, neurogenesis, neuroinflammatory response, and default mode network connectivity, all of which are linked to depression and dementia. Preclinical research studies demonstrate that psilocybin increases hippocampal plasticity, restores dendritic complexity, lowers proinflammatory cytokine levels, and promotes fear extinction in experimental models of stress, ischemic stroke, and neurodegeneration. Emerging clinical studies also indicate that individuals with moderate cognitive impairment, early-onset Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease may see long-term decreases in anxiety and depression as well as improvements in cognitive function, frequently after a single dose administration. Additionally, psilocybin has demonstrated promise in treating mental comorbidities that often accompany neurodegenerative illness, such as treatment-resistant depression, drug use disorders, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. However, there are still significant obstacles to overcome, such as optimizing dosing schedules, assessing safety issues such as temporary perceptual abnormalities and cardiovascular consequences, and translating preclinical results into extensive phase -III clinical studies. This review incorporates the most recent data on psilocybin's chemistry, pharmacology, metabolism, and mechanistic actions; it highlights the drug's therapeutic potential across a variety of neurodegenerative diseases and emphasizes the necessity of carefully planned randomized controlled trials to determine clinical efficacy, long-term safety, and its place in multimodal treatment approaches.

papers.title: Gut microbial and metabolomic alterations associated with herpetic trigeminal neuralgia: an exploratory multi-omics study.
papers.abstract: Herpetic trigeminal neuralgia (HTN) is a neuropathic pain disorder caused by varicella-zoster virus invasion of the trigeminal nerve, but its mechanisms remain poorly elucidated. Accumulating evidence implicates gut microbiota dysbiosis and metabolic perturbations in modulating chronic pain via the gut-brain axis, yet their roles in HTN have not been systematically explored. Integrated multi-omics analysis was performed on 19 patients with HTN and 18 healthy controls. Fecal metagenomic sequencing characterized gut microbial composition and function. Untargeted metabolomics profiled metabolic signatures in fecal and circulating samples. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and random forest modeling screened pivotal microbial and metabolic features associated with HTN. Correlation analysis between differential metabolites and clinical pain scores validated the translational potential of identified alterations. HTN patients showed significantly reduced gut microbial diversity, with enriched Proteobacteria , depleted butyrate-producing bacteria (including Faecalibacterium , Roseburia , and Lachnospira ), and expanded opportunistic pathogens ( Escherichia coli and [ Ruminococcus ] gnavus ). Microbial pathways for pH homeostasis and oxidative stress defense were downregulated. Metabolomic analysis identified differential metabolites, primarily involving nicotinate/nicotinamide metabolism and retrograde endocannabinoid signaling. WGCNA and random forest analyses suggested fecal metabolites as potential candidate features, with associations between gut microbial dysregulation and systemic metabolic changes. Furthermore, screened metabolites correlated significantly with pain scores. This study provides multi-omics evidence of gut microbial and metabolic dysregulation in HTN, generating hypotheses for further mechanistic research. Large-scale, multicenter prospective cohorts with standardized metadata collection are needed to validate these findings.

papers.title: Advances in the Anatomy, Histology, and Embryology of the Dromedary (Camelus dromedarius) Brain and Spinal Cord.
papers.abstract: The dromedary (Camelus dromedarius) represents a remarkable model of physiological and anatomical adaptation to extreme environments. While many researchers have focused on its unique metabolic and water-conserving abilities, the neuroscience underlying these adaptations are noticeable unexplored. This study reviews the latest findings in the anatomy, histology, and embryology of the dromedary nervous system. It highlights the gross and comparative neuroanatomy, emphasizing distinctive features of the central, peripheral and autonomic nervous systems, including the complex cerebral vasculature. Histological studies demonstrate a diverse array of neuronal and glial cell types in the caudate nucleus, cerebellum and spinal trigeminal nucleus, reflecting advanced neural processing. Furthermore, embryological investigations trace the development of the nervous system from neurulation and the formation of brain vesicles. Finally, this review connects these neurobiological features to the camel's unique adaptations, such as thermoregulation and pain perception, and discusses the implications of emerging technologies such as nanobody-based therapies derived from camelids for treating neurological disorders. This comprehensive overview underscores the camel as a vital subject for neuroscientific research, offering novel perspectives on neural structure, function and evolution in response to environmental pressures.

papers.title: Microplastics as Microbiota Modulators: Rewiring the Gut Metabolism Immune Axis.
papers.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) have emerged as pervasive environmental contaminants with increasing relevance to human health. Beyond their role as inert particulate pollutants, accumulating evidence suggests that MPs may act as biologically active modulators of the gastrointestinal ecosystem. The gut represents a major interface for MP exposure, where ingested particles interact with intestinal epithelial cells, mucus layers, immune components, and resident microbial communities. This review summarizes current evidence on MPs' capacity to alter gut microbiota composition, impair intestinal barrier integrity, disrupt microbial metabolite production, and promote inflammatory and metabolic disturbances.Experimental studies indicate that MP exposure may reduce microbial diversity, shift the abundance of key bacterial taxa, impair tight junction proteins, and increase intestinal permeability. These changes may facilitate the translocation of bacterial products such as lipopolysaccharide, thereby activating inflammatory pathways including TLR4/NF-κB signaling. In parallel, MP-associated dysbiosis may alter short-chain fatty acids, bile acid metabolism, and tryptophan-derived metabolites, suggesting plausible biological pathways relevant to insulin resistance, hepatic lipid dysregulation, cardiometabolic risk, and gut-brain axis disruption. However, most available evidence is derived from animal and in vitro models, and causal relationships in humans remain insufficiently established. Major limitations include heterogeneous exposure protocols, non-standardized particle characterization, limited human longitudinal data, and difficulty separating particle-specific effects from those of associated chemical contaminants.Future studies integrating environmentally realistic exposure models, standardized microbiome analyses, multi-omics approaches, and human cohort designs are needed. Overall, the gut microbiota may represent a critical biological interface through which MPs interact with host physiology; however, further evidence is required before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding their role in human chronic disease susceptibility.

papers.title: Molecular mechanism of total flavonoids of hawthorn leaves in spinal cord injury treatment: A combined network pharmacology and experimental study.
papers.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating neurological disorder characterized by irreversible motor and sensory dysfunction, largely driven by secondary injury mechanisms including oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis. Total flavonoids of hawthorn leaves (TFHL), a traditional Chinese medicine, have demonstrated antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties; however, their therapeutic effects and mechanisms in SCI remain unclear. Network pharmacology was employed to identify the active compounds, potential targets, and key signaling pathways of TFHL in SCI through target prediction, protein-protein interaction analysis, and GO and KEGG enrichment analyses. Experimental validation was performed using a rat SCI model, LPS-stimulated BV-2 microglial cells, and RAW264.7 macrophages. Functional recovery was assessed by BBB scoring, while histopathological changes, ultrastructural alterations, inflammatory cytokine expression, and MAPK pathway activation were evaluated using H&amp;E staining, transmission electron microscopy, RT-qPCR, and western blotting. Network pharmacology analysis identified 15 active compounds and 69 overlapping therapeutic targets, mainly enriched in pathways related to inflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and neuronal survival, including MAPK, PI3K-Akt, TNF, and NF-kB signaling pathways. In vivo , TFHL treatment significantly improved locomotor recovery, alleviated histological damage, preserved mitochondrial structure, and reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines following SCI. In vitro, TFHL markedly suppressed LPS-induced activation of the MAPK pathway in microglial cells. TFHL improves functional and histopathological outcomes in SCI models and attenuates inflammatory activation. These effects are consistent with multi-pathway regulation predicted by network pharmacology and are supported, at least in part, by MAPK pathway suppression, warranting further mechanistic and translational studies.

papers.title: Alternative splicing of a species- and skeletal muscle-specific microexon diversifies the menu of clathrin heavy chains in mice and rats.
papers.abstract: Little is known about alternative splicing of microexons in most tissues other than the brain. Humans have two homologous clathrin heavy chains. Ubiquitously expressed, CLTC drives clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Highly expressed in skeletal muscles, CLTCL1 instead regulates glucose metabolism. Previously, we reported that a conserved microexon (exon 31) in the CLTC gene is alternatively spliced during striated muscle development. Here, we identified a novel Cltc microexon (exon 33, hereafter microexon 33), which is only included in mouse and rat adult skeletal muscles. Microexon 33 inclusion shortens the CLTC C-terminus and adds 10 distinct terminal residues. This divergence occurs at the same position at which the human CLTCL1 constitutively includes its penultimate exon (another microexon). CLTCL1 is a pseudogene in mice and rats. Humans diversified the menu of clathrin heavy chains by gene duplication and tissue-specific gene expression, whereas mice and rats might have achieved similar diversification by tissue-specific regulation of Cltc alternative splicing.

papers.title: Predictive Factors of Abnormal Brain CT Scan in Patients with Opioid Poisoning: A Single-Center Study.
papers.abstract: Opioid poisoning is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly in Iran; however, no clear guidelines exist regarding the appropriate timing for non-contrast BCTS in these patients. This study aims to identify clinical and laboratory factors that predict abnormal BCTS findings in individuals with opioid poisoning. We conducted the study among patients presenting to the emergency department of Shiraz Namazi Hospital with opioid poisoning. This retrospective cross-sectional study was performed on 208 patients with opioid poisoning who were referred to the emergency department of Namazi Hospital between March 2019 and March 2021. Data collection involved accessing the archives of Namazi Hospital to gather the necessary information for this study. Among 208 patients with opioid poisoning who underwent brain CT, 57 (27.4%) exhibited abnormal BCTS findings within this selected subgroup. Multivariable logistic regression identified two independent predictive factors for abnormal BCTS: advanced age (OR 1.041 per year; 95% CI 1.01-1.07; P =0.008) and lower serum bicarbonate (OR 0.908 per mEq/L; 95% CI 0.83-0.99; P =0.025). The most prevalent abnormal findings included microvascular ischemic damage, followed by ischemic infarctions. Advanced age and lower serum bicarbonate levels are independent predictors of abnormal BCTS findings in patients with acute opioid poisoning. Clinicians should consider urgent BCTS in older patients or those with metabolic acidosis, as these groups are at higher risk and may derive the greatest benefit from emergent neuroimaging.

papers.title: Central relaxin-3/RXFP3 signaling potently drives orexigenic behaviors and attenuates cisplatin-induced anorexia and body weight loss.
papers.abstract: The relaxin-3 neuropeptide system promotes energy balance by increasing feeding behavior. Here, we investigate the behavioral mechanisms mediating the orexigenic effects of relaxin-3 and the therapeutic potential of relaxin-3 to combat metabolic disorders. We show that central and peripheral administration of relaxin-3 increases high-fat diet intake by increasing meal size in obese rats. Furthermore, we deleted relaxin family peptide receptor 3 (RXFP3) neuronally using RXFP3 fl/fl hSyn-Cre+ mice and show that neuronal RXFP3 is required for the orexigenic effects of relaxin-3. In addition, central relaxin-3 administration augmented food motivation for sucrose and hyperphagia in a binge-like eating model. We then evaluated the potential of relaxin-3 to drive food intake in rats receiving acute maladaptive chemotherapy. Pretreatment of central relaxin-3 attenuated cisplatin chemotherapy-induced anorexia and body weight loss. These findings characterize the behavioral mechanisms by which the relaxin-3 system drives feeding behaviors and highlight its therapeutic potential for metabolic wasting disorders.

papers.title: Why only 3 months? Immunological constraints on CAR-T therapy in gastrointestinal cancers.
papers.abstract: In June 2026, satri-cel/CT041, a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell product targeting Claudin18.2, received approval from China's National Medical Products Administration for the treatment of Claudin18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma after failure of at least two prior lines of therapy. This marks the first CAR-T product approved worldwide for solid tumours. The approval ends the long-standing debate over whether CAR-T cells can be effective against solid malignancies, yet it simultaneously raises a more pointed issue: in its pivotal randomised controlled trial, median progression-free survival was 3.25 months (95% CI 2.86-4.53) with satri-cel against 1.77 months (95% CI 1.61-2.04) with treatment of physician's choice, giving a hazard ratio of 0.37 (95% CI 0.24-0.56). The two medians differ by 1.48 months; that figure marks where each survival distribution is cut in half and is not the benefit any individual patient can expect, and approval does not equate to a cure. Taking this as a starting point, this review systematically dissects the immunological bottlenecks that constrain CAR-T efficacy in gastrointestinal tumours. We first trace the evidence chain from phase I studies through the randomised controlled trial to exploratory adjuvant-therapy settings and then integrate the landscape of targets-Claudin18.2, glypican-3, carcinoembryonic antigen, mesothelin, and CDH17-within a target-tumour matrix encompassing gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and pancreatic cancer. The core section focuses on four intertwined immunological constraints: spatiotemporal heterogeneity and escape at the antigen level; a therapeutic window shaped jointly by epitope masking within tight junctions and immune privilege of the gastric mucosal stem cell niche-this mechanism not only explains why Claudin18.2-directed CAR-T cells exhibit an acceptable safety profile despite target expression on normal tissues but also provides a paradigm for rational selection of next-generation targets; a suppressive microenvironment composed of regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, tumour-associated macrophages, transforming growth factor-β, adenosine, and a hypoxic and acidotic metabolic milieu; and CAR-T exhaustion driven by chronic antigen stimulation. We particularly emphasise that metabolic stress and exhaustion are not two parallel obstacles. We put forward a mechanistic model in which persistent antigen stimulation combined with intratumoral hypoxia acts as a "double hit": through mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species accumulation, the two inputs raise nuclear factor of activated T-cell (NFAT) activity and so drive the TOX/NR4A-dominated exhaustion program. This model is assembled from chronic-infection and mouse tumour systems and has not been tested in human CAR-T cells or in satri-cel-treated patients. We advance it as a framework for organising the four bottlenecks and for explaining why single-point interventions struggle to lift the efficacy ceiling, not as a demonstrated account. On this basis, we discuss strategies such as armouring, logic gating, transcription factor engineering, gene editing, and chemokine receptor modification, along with combination regimens involving checkpoint inhibition, oncolytic viruses, locoregional administration, and microbiome modulation, and we evaluate alternative platforms including CAR-macrophages, CAR-NK cells, and in vivo CAR-T generation. The watershed has been crossed, but the work of turning 3 months into 30 has only just begun.

papers.title: Gut microbiome-shaped chemotherapy responses across cancer types: mechanisms of resistance, biomarkers, and targeted interventions.
papers.abstract: Cytotoxic chemotherapy remains an important component of multimodal treatment for many solid tumors, but resistance and dose-limiting toxicities continue to constrain clinical benefit. The gut microbiome can influence chemotherapy response through microbial drug biotransformation, metabolite signaling, intestinal-barrier integrity, systemic immune regulation, and tumor-cell stress and death pathways. Across solid tumors, the evidence is strongest in colorectal cancer, where clinical associations are supported by increasingly detailed mechanistic and interventional studies; evidence in many extraintestinal cancers remains less mature and is dominated by smaller observational cohorts and selected preclinical models. Importantly, gut-derived systemic effects should be distinguished from local or tumor-associated microbial mechanisms, and direct tumor-cell resistance should be separated from altered drug exposure and toxicity-mediated reductions in relative dose intensity. Microbiota-associated and metabolic biomarkers and microbiota-targeted interventions show potential for treatment stratification, toxicity prediction, and therapeutic modulation, but clinical translation remains limited by heterogeneous cohorts, incomplete causal validation, variable engraftment and strain specificity, and safety and standardization requirements. Overall, the microbiome is best viewed as a cancer- and regimen-specific modifier of chemotherapy rather than a universal determinant of response. Prospective, mechanism-matched studies are needed to establish whether microbiome-guided strategies can improve treatment efficacy, tolerance, and completion.

papers.title: Lipid metabolism: a potential checkpoint for cGAS-STING regulation in colorectal cancer.
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy for colorectal cancer (CRC) continues to face significant challenges, particularly in patients with microsatellite stable (MSS) tumors. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway is a key regulator of innate immunity and has emerged as a promising target for enhancing anti-tumor immune responses. Meanwhile, lipid metabolic reprogramming is a defining hallmark of CRC and contributes to tumor progression, evasion, and therapeutic resistance. Although direct evidence linking lipid metabolism to cGAS-STING signaling in CRC remains limited, accumulating studies from diverse disease models suggest extensive interactions between these two processes. This review summarizes the major features of lipid metabolic reprogramming in CRC and discusses current understanding of cGAS-STING signaling in tumor immunity. We further examine potential mechanisms by which lipid metabolism may influence cGAS-STING activity, including the regulation of mitochondrial DNA release, intracellular trafficking of signaling components and lipid-associated post-translational modifications. Emerging evidence also indicates that cGAS-STING signaling can affect lipid metabolic pathways by regulating lipid metabolic homeostasis and inducing lipid peroxidation-driven ferroptosis. Importantly, microbiota-derived lipid metabolites exert context-dependent effects on cGAS-STING signaling to balance intestinal inflammation and anti-tumor immunity. Finally, we discuss therapeutic strategies targeting lipid metabolism and cGAS-STING signaling, with a particular focus on approaches that may enhance anti-tumor immunity through coordinated metabolic-immune modulation. By bridging metabolic reprogramming with innate immune sensing, we propose that modulating the lipid-cGAS-STING axis could break immune tolerance and offer a distinct therapeutic window for CRC.

papers.title: GART expression is associated with a proliferative and purine-metabolic ISC-like epithelial state in ulcerative colitis.
papers.abstract: To characterize the epithelial state associated with GART expression in ulcerative colitis (UC) and determine whether this association reflects a GART-specific program or a broader proliferative and purine-metabolic phenotype. Four independent bulk transcriptomic cohorts were analyzed and synthesized by random-effects meta-analysis. Human colonic scRNA-seq datasets (GSE214695 and SCP259) were integrated, with principal comparisons repeated using donor-aware pseudobulk or mixed-effects approaches and adjustment for sequencing depth, gene detection, and cell-cycle covariates. GART detection was defined from raw counts and tested using alternative thresholds. Pseudotime, scTenifoldKnk, CellChat/LIANA, and transcriptional-network analyses were used as exploratory analyses. Spatial transcriptomics (GSE189184), human colonic multiplex immunofluorescence, and acute DSS-induced colitis tissues were used for tissue-level localization. Across the four bulk cohorts, GART expression showed an overall increase in UC (pooled Hedges' g = 0.743, 95% CI 0.239-1.248; P = 0.0183). In the single-cell atlas, GART detection localized preferentially to an ISC-like epithelial compartment, although the magnitude of the UC-associated detection difference varied between cohorts. Within UC ISC-like cells, donor-paired pseudobulk analyses identified proliferative and nucleotide-metabolic transcriptional differences associated with GART detection. Across the broader ISC-like epithelial atlas, donor-aware module analyses showed positive associations of GART detection with purine-biosynthesis, DNA-replication, DNA-repair, and mitotic programs, and these associations remained positive within cell-cycle strata. Comparison with other de novo purine-synthesis enzymes did not support a uniquely GART-specific alteration. Exploratory network analyses linked the GART-associated state to proliferative and nucleotide-metabolic programs but did not establish functional dependence. In seven independent spatial donors, the single-cell-derived epithelial program was consistently higher in GART-detected than GART-undetected epithelial regions (mean within-donor difference = 0.0262, 95% CI 0.0140-0.0407; exact P = 0.0156). Human tissue immunofluorescence further showed co-enrichment of GART with OLFM4-positive ISC-like, MYBL2/Ki67-positive proliferative, and MIF/CD74-associated inflammatory regions across the corresponding panel-specific participant sets. GART identifies a proliferative and purine-metabolic ISC-like epithelial state in UC but is not established as a specific driver of epithelial regeneration. The findings support an association between GART detection, nucleotide-demand programs, proliferative epithelial activity, and the inflammatory tissue context, providing a framework for future direct functional studies.

papers.title: When do starch-polyphenol complexes qualify as type 5 resistant starch? A critical evidence framework from molecular assembly to colonic utilization.
papers.abstract: Starch-polyphenol complexes are increasingly explored for modulating starch digestibility, developing low-glycemic-index foods, and improving polyphenol stability and delivery. Some systems have been described as type 5 resistant starch (RS5) or RS5-like based on V-type crystalline signals, increased resistant starch content, or reduced glucose release. However, these outcomes alone are insufficient for RS5 assignment because they may also arise from surface adsorption, non-inclusion networks, substrate shielding, enzyme inhibition by free or released polyphenols, or food-matrix effects. This review critically assesses the evidence required to describe starch-polyphenol systems as V-type starch-polyphenol complexes with demonstrated enzymatic resistance and examines their relationship to the proposed non-lipid extension of RS5. Evidence from molecular assembly, structural characterization, processing-induced rearrangement, resistance to enzymatic digestion, polyphenol release, colonic fermentation, and physiological relevance is integrated. V-type or V-type-like inclusion provides the strongest structural basis for identifying a V-type starch-polyphenol complex, whereas surface-bound complexes, non-inclusion networks and covalent derivatives require different mechanistic descriptions. Mechanistic attribution should include removal and quantification of unbound polyphenols, physical-mixture and washed-complex controls, and enzyme-inhibition kinetics. A tiered evidence framework is proposed to classify these systems as putative RS5, RS5-like complexes, polyphenol-bound resistant starch candidates, enzyme-inhibition-dominated systems, or non-RS mixtures.

papers.title: NUAK isoforms promote glucose and glutamine metabolic reprogramming driven colon cancer progression and migration through regulation of AMPK/mTOR signaling.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) cells undergo significant alterations in glucose and glutamine metabolism to support rapid growth and migration. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these metabolic changes remain incompletely understood. Although NUAK1 and NUAK2, members of the NUAK kinase family have been implicated in CRC tumorigenesis, their specific roles in metabolic reprogramming that drives CRC progression and metastasis have not been elucidated. In this study, we demonstrate that NUAK1 and NUAK2 are overexpressed in human CRC tissues and that their expression is associated with increased tumor metastasis and poorer patient survival. NUAK1/2 promotes CRC cell proliferation and migration, whereas their depletion markedly reduces cell growth and migratory capacity. Furthermore, knockout of NUAK1/2 disrupts key metabolic pathways, including aerobic glycolysis, pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), and glutamine metabolism. Mechanistically, NUAK1/2 facilitates mTOR-driven metabolic reprogramming and promotes CRC growth and migration by suppressing AMPK activity. Depletion of NUAK1/2 impairs metabolic function, cellular growth, and migration potential in CRC cells, effects that are further enhanced by pharmacological activation of AMPK with AICAR and inhibition of mTOR using Rapamycin. In conclusion, these findings identify NUAK1/2 as critical regulators of CRC progression and migration through AMPK/mTOR-mediated metabolic reprogramming, highlighting their potential as therapeutic targets in colorectal cancer.

papers.title: Implementing single-port robotic platform into your colorectal surgery practice: a SAGES colorectal committee task force review of evolving robotic technology and innovations-Part II.
papers.abstract: Transanal surgery has advanced significantly since the introduction of transanal endoscopic microsurgery (TEM) in 1983. The single-port (SP) robotic system marks the latest technological advancement in minimally invasive transanal surgery, combining single-site access with full robotic articulation through a single 25 mm port. This is the first video dynamic manuscript and 2nd document of a four-part SAGES Colorectal Committee series outlining the foundational application of SP technology in colorectal surgery, specifically transanal minimally invasive surgery (SP-TAMIS). The SAGES Colorectal Committee SP Task Force performed a structured review of the da Vinci SP system, assessing platform features, instrumentation, and workflow considerations for transanal surgery. Task force members (subject matter experts with early experience with single-port robotic platforms) analyzed technical details, patient selection, operative workflows, and early outcomes. Representative procedural video-based techniques were detailed with emphasis on instrumentation, docking, and key operative steps specific to the SP transanal procedure. The SP platform appears to offer several technological advantages for transanal surgery: (1) natural hand-eye coordination in an inverted field, (2) enhanced visualization with an articulating cobra camera, and (3) a third arm for retraction and exposure. These features appear to improve precision, reduce collision risk and fatigue, and shorten operative time. Published early clinical data suggest low positive margin rates (≈ 4-5%) and acceptable morbidity for multiport robotic TAMIS/SP-TAMIS in selected patients. However, direct comparative evidence versus conventional TAMIS remains limited, and many comparisons are indirect across heterogeneous cohorts. Current limitations include high cost, limited distal reach, lack of dedicated energy devices, and learning curve. The learning curve appears to be shorter than for laparoscopic TAMIS. Peritoneal entry during full-thickness excision of upper rectal and anterior lesions is a recognized event in transanal surgery; the SP platform offers several features that may facilitate its management, though SP-specific incidence data are not yet available. SME early experience with SP-TAMIS suggests that it can provide a safe, effective, and ergonomically superior method for local rectal excision. Mastery of this foundational application builds the skills needed for more complex SP colorectal procedures, with the potential for single-port robotics expansion into minimally invasive colorectal surgery through enhanced precision, reduced invasiveness, and improved surgeon ergonomics.

papers.title: Disentangling microbiota-dependent and -independent impacts of antibiotics on host physiology.
papers.abstract: Antibiotics are believed to affect host physiology by altering the gut microbiota. However, it remains unclear which effects of antibiotics are microbiota dependent and which are microbiota independent. Here we present a resource encompassing host and microbiota responses to antibiotic treatment and a computational tool with which to analyse them. Metagenomic and transcriptomic analyses of conventional and germ-free mice revealed that antibiotic administration routes and their combinations affect host and microbiota responses. We developed CompoRes-a computational tool that distinguishes the microbiota-independent impact of antibiotic-induced perturbations, revealing that antibiotics directly impact host physiology. We found that diurnal expression of major histocompatibility complex class II in the mouse colon is controlled by glucose via feeding. This pattern was lost during antibiotic treatment as vancomycin altered feeding behaviour in a microbiota-independent and evolutionarily conserved manner. Together, our study establishes a direct, non-microbial pathway by which antibiotics reshape host immunity and circadian physiology.

papers.title: Matrix stiffness promotes colorectal cancer progression via Golgi-dependent cholesterol synthesis.
papers.abstract: Extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffening and metabolic reprogramming are hallmarks of colorectal cancer (CRC) progression; however, the mechanistic link between biomechanical cues and cholesterol metabolism remains poorly defined. Here, we delineate a mechano-metabolic pathway in which matrix stiffness activates the mechanosensitive Ca²⁺ channel Piezo1 to drive structural reorganization of the Golgi apparatus, promoting its close apposition with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This organelle remodeling facilitates the proteolytic activation and nuclear translocation of SREBP2, thereby transcriptionally upregulating HMGCR, the rate-limiting enzyme for cholesterol synthesis, and elevating intracellular cholesterol. HMGCR upregulation is functionally essential for stiffness-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and CRC progression. Mechanistically, HMGCR-mediated cholesterol accumulation promotes phosphorylation of β-catenin at Ser552, which disrupts β-catenin/E-cadherin complexes at adherens junctions, leading to β-catenin nuclear accumulation and EMT execution. Therapeutically, combined pharmacological inhibition of matrix crosslinking and cholesterol synthesis synergistically suppresses tumor growth and invasion while restoring epithelial architecture in vivo. Collectively, these findings reveal that Piezo1-dependent Golgi-ER reorganization triggers SREBP2-driven cholesterol synthesis, ultimately fueling β-catenin-mediated junctional disassembly and metastasis, and highlight the therapeutic promise of co-targeting tumor mechanics and metabolism.

papers.title: 2'-Fucosyllactose enhances indole-3-lactic acid production by Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 and alleviates colitis-associated bone loss: Associations with microbiota remodeling and intestinal AHR-related responses.
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease is frequently associated with an imbalance in bone remodeling and a decline in bone mass, however, there is a lack of systematic research on microbiome-based intervention strategies targeting colitis-associated bone loss. In this study, Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 (DNG-08) was selected from four candidate strains based on its favorable 2'-fucosyllactose (2'-FL) utilization and indole-3-lactic acid (ILA) production. Genomic annotation revealed that DNG-08 harbors functional genes related to fucosylated oligosaccharide utilization and the conversion of tryptophan to ILA. In a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model, combined intervention with DNG-08 and 2'-FL significantly alleviated colitis-associated phenotypes, and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels by 13.33%-58.69%, while increasing IL-10-1.23 times that of the DSS group. Simultaneously, the combined intervention improved trabecular bone microstructure, increasing the bone formation marker procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP) by 14.61%-56.37%, decreasing the bone resorption marker C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX-I) by 17.03%-21.77%, and upregulating the expression of Wnt3a, β-catenin, and Runx2. Gut microbiota analysis showed that combined intervention could partially reverse DSS-induced dysbiosis, enriching potentially beneficial bacterial taxa while reducing inflammation-associated genera. Notably, combined treatment group exhibited elevated serum ILA levels, increased colonic aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) fluorescence, and upregulatied CYP1A1 expression. Correlation analysis identified significant associations among serum ILA, AHR-related indicators, selected bacterial genera, and bone remodeling parameters. This study highlights that strain-substrate matching may serve as a precise synbiotic strategy to improve inflammation-related gut-bone axis dysfunction.

papers.title: Integrating Non-Invasive Liver Assessment into Screening Colonoscopy: A Prospective Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Steatotic liver disease is underdiagnosed despite guideline recommendations for risk-based case-finding. Colorectal cancer (CRC) screening colonoscopy engages a prevention-oriented, healthcare-seeking population in whom liver disease may go undetected. We assessed the feasibility, acceptance, and yield of non-invasive liver assessment integrated into screening colonoscopy visits. This prospective cross-sectional study enrolled adults aged ≥50 years attending screening colonoscopy. Individuals with known chronic liver disease were excluded. Participants underwent hepatic ultrasound and point shear wave elastography.
