Supportive nutrition, exercise, and symptom management rarely restore lean mass, function, or treatment tolerance once wasting is established. Ferroptosis, iron-dependent cell death caused by phospholipid peroxidation, may connect inflammatory iron redistribution, lipid remodeling, mitochondrial stress, and impaired antioxidant defenses. This review critically evaluates ferroptosis in cachexia from a tumor-host pharmacology perspective, distinguishing causal evidence from associated oxidative signatures. We highlight two experimentally supported mechanisms: neutrophil-derived lipocalin-2 in lung cancer cachexia and tumor exosomal miR-203a-3p in pancreatic cancer-associated muscle wasting. We also examine the paradox that tumor ferroptosis induction may weaken host-tissue resistance and worsen muscle and adipose loss. We propose a "split-ferroptosis" strategy combining tumor sensitization with host-protective iron modulation, lipid peroxide scavenging, endogenous defense reinforcement, and biomarker-guided patient selection to expand the tumor-host therapeutic index.

papers.title: Living Donor Liver Transplantation for Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide-Secreting Tumors with Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria Syndrome Resulting from Transformation of a Nonfunctional Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumor with Multiple Liver Metastases: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs) are a rare subtype of neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs), some of which cause characteristic clinical syndromes due to hormone hypersecretion. Vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting tumors (VIPomas) produce vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) and are associated with watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA) syndrome, often leading to severe treatment-refractory symptoms. Although liver transplantation (LT) is regarded as a promising option for unresectable, liver-limited NENs, studies focusing on VIPoma remain limited, as do reports of transformation from nonfunctional pancreatic NENs (PNENs) to VIPoma. Furthermore, to the best of our knowledge, no cases have described progression to LT after such a transformation. Therefore, we report this case. A 65-year-old woman with nonfunctional PNEN G2 and multiple liver metastases underwent multimodal treatment including a multi-kinase inhibitor, somatostatin analogs, a mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors, and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). During treatment, the tumor acquired VIP-secreting capacity and transformed into a VIPoma, resulting in WDHA syndrome characterized by intractable watery diarrhea, severe electrolyte imbalance, and metabolic acidosis. Because neither conservative management nor debulking surgery achieved adequate symptom control, and no extrahepatic disease was identified, living donor LT (LDLT) was performed. After transplantation, the diarrhea resolved promptly, and no recurrence has been observed 1 year post-transplantation. We report a rare case in which a nonfunctional PNEN transformed into a VIPoma during the clinical course, leading to severe WDHA syndrome. LDLT for liver-limited disease may represent an effective therapeutic option for both tumor control and symptom relief in carefully selected patients.

papers.title: The lipotoxicity-ferroptosis axis in the transition from insulin resistance to type 2 diabetes: mechanistic integration and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.abstract: Insulin resistance is an early feature of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but progression to persistent hyperglycemia requires failure of pancreatic β-cell compensation. Lipotoxicity develops when adipose storage and oxidative capacity are exceeded, increasing fatty-acid flux and accumulation of ceramides, diacylglycerols, and oxidizable phospholipids in liver, skeletal muscle, and pancreatic islets. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by uncontrolled phospholipid peroxidation. Lipotoxicity can increase ferroptosis susceptibility by enriching polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane phospholipids, increasing organelle-derived reactive oxygen species, and weakening system Xc--glutathione-glutathione peroxidase 4 defense; however, expansion of a redox-active iron pool is a distinct, cell- and context-dependent requirement. We organize these processes into a four-state working model spanning metabolic compensation, systemic lipid overflow and insulin resistance, ferroptosis sensitization, and β-cell decompensation. This is a non-obligate conceptual trajectory rather than a universally recognized clinical sequence. Evidence is strongest in pancreatic β-cell and liver models; direct skeletal-muscle causality is limited, and a causal role in human T2DM has not been established. Ferroptosis also has cell-specific effects: protecting β cells may be beneficial, whereas ferroptotic removal of selected inflammatory or lipid-storing cell populations can improve metabolic outcomes in some models. Upstream lipid unloading through weight loss and established metabolic treatments has the greatest clinical maturity. ACSL4/LPCAT3-dependent membrane remodeling, GPX4-centered defense, ferritinophagy, labile iron, parallel suppressor systems, and targeted delivery remain predominantly preclinical or candidate approaches. Multidimensional biomarker panels may support future mechanistic studies, but no individual marker or composite panel is currently validated to diagnose ferroptosis or a ferroptosis-susceptible phenotype in T2DM. The lipotoxicity-ferroptosis axis should therefore be viewed as a testable, tissue-specific amplifier rather than a universal or solitary cause of T2DM.

papers.title: Amelioration of chronic inflammation, insulin resistance, and gut microbiota homeostasis by a combination of Bifidobacterium , Lactobacillus , Enterococcus , and Bacillus in obese type 2 diabetic mice.
papers.abstract: To examine the effects of a combination of live Bifidobacterium , Lactobacillus , Enterococcus , and Bacillus (CBLEB) on glucose/lipid metabolism, inflammation, gut microbiota, and related mechanisms in obese type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) mice. Obese T2DM mice were established by feeding mice a high-fat diet for four weeks, followed by a single intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin (100 mg/kg). The mice were then divided randomly into 5 groups (n = 8/group): normal control (NC), T2DM model, CBLEB (585 mg/kg/d, by gavage), dimethylbiguanide (DMBG, 200 mg/kg/d, by gavage), and CBLEB+DMBG combination. All treatments were administered daily for four weeks. The body weight and fasting blood glucose were monitored weekly. An oral glucose tolerance test was performed to assess the glucose tolerance. The serum levels of lipids (triglycerides, total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol), insulin, and inflammatory factors (tumor necrosis factor [TNF]-α, interleukin [IL]-1β, IL-6, IL-10, and lipopolysaccharide) were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Pancreatic IL-6 and TNF-α expression was detected by immunohistochemistry. The histopathological changes in the pancreas, colon, and adipose tissues were evaluated by hematoxylin and eosin staining. The protein expression of insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS-1)/p-IRS-1 (Ser307), Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/MyD88, tight junction proteins (zonula occludens protein 1 [ZO-1]/claudin 1 [CLDN1]/occludin), and B-cell lymphoma/leukemia-2 (Bcl-2)-associated X protein A (BAX)/Bcl-2 was analyzed by Western blot. The gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. CBLEB significantly improved the weight gain, hyperglycemia, insulin resistance (IR), dyslipidemia, reduced adipocyte size, suppressed systemic inflammation, and alleviated pancreatic and colonic damage in T2DM mice. The combination of CBLEB and DMBG showed the most pronounced improvements in metabolic and inflammatory parameters. Western blot showed that CBLEB inhibited TLR4/MyD88 signaling, enhanced insulin signaling (IRS-1/p-IRS-1), repaired the intestinal barrier (ZO-1/CLDN1/occludin), and regulated the apoptotic balance (BAX/Bcl-2). Gut microbiota analysis suggested that CBLEB remodeled the gut microbiota, with a functional prediction suggesting shifts in the metabolic pathways and a decrease in the abundance of Escherichia spp. CBLEB ameliorated systemic inflammation and IR in obese T2DM mice through gut microbiota modulation, intestinal barrier restoration, and suppression of inflammatory pathways.

papers.title: Type 1 diabetes metabolomics and multi-omics: Current applications, limitations, and future directions - A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is an autoimmune disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic β-cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency and lifelong dependence on exogenous insulin. This disease, if not treated, leads to acute and chronic complications affecting the cardiovascular, renal, and retinal systems and introduces significant psychosocial burdens. But even with advances in insulin therapy, optimal glycemic control remains difficult to achieve. T1DM progression spans from autoantibody seroconversion to overt diabetes, accompanied by dynamic metabolic perturbations, contributing to β-cell dysfunction. These metabolic alterations correlate with glycemic markers and provide integrated signatures of gene-environment interactions and disease heterogeneity. Therefore, metabolomics has emerged as a promising approach for identifying metabolic dysregulation associated with T1DM, with some studies reporting metabolite alterations detectable before clinical onset or autoantibody positivity; targeted and untargeted approaches enable comprehensive profiling of disease-associated metabolic pathways, although these findings largely reflect associations from observational cohorts rather than validated early-detection tools. Here, the analysis of biofluids with advanced platforms such as UPLC-MS and NMR provides high-resolution insights into systemic metabolism, supporting the discovery of candidate biomarkers that may, pending further validation, contribute to earlier diagnosis and precision medicine strategies in T1DM. Even though current metabolomic studies have substantially improved the classification of metabolic alterations associated with T1DM, the field still necessitates clarification of causal mechanisms, standardization of methodologies, validation of findings across diverse populations, and integration of metabolomics with other omics platforms in robust longitudinal designs. These gaps highlight a clear necessity of moving beyond descriptive profiling toward systematically standardized and validated metabolomic markers embedded within multi-omics and longitudinal frameworks.

papers.title: REG family proteins and immune regulation: current evidence and perspectives.
papers.abstract: As a group of small secretory proteins widely expressed in digestive and nondigestive tissues, the regenerating islet-derived (REG) family members have been highlighted for their multifunctional properties, such as pro-proliferative, mitogenic, anti-apoptotic, differentiation-inducing, anti-inflammatory, bactericidal, anti-oxidation and pro-tissue-repair activities. Emerging evidence indicates context-dependent immunomodulatory potentials of specific REG proteins. This review focused on the involvement and potential roles of REG family proteins in regulating immune cells. Available data suggest that individual REG members, including human REG4/murine Reg4, specific REG3/Reg3 subfamily isoforms, and murine Reg2, exert heterogeneous regulatory effects on macrophage migration, recruitment, proliferation, and function. The immunomodulatory impacts of REG3/Reg3 subfamily members on dendritic cell phenotype and function have recently been uncovered in pancreatic carcinogenesis and autoimmune diabetic models. Certain REG proteins also exhibit context-dependent modulatory effects on T cell and neutrophil responses, though current observations remain fragmentary. Research regarding REG-mediated immune regulation is still in its infancy, with undefined cellular receptors, ambiguous direct targets, and incompletely resolved signaling mechanisms. Further mechanistic validation is therefore required before the translational potential of REG-based immunotherapies for inflammatory and immunological diseases can be reliably evaluated.

papers.title: Beyond Digestion: Secretin as a Key Regulator of Systemic pH.
papers.abstract: Secretin is a broad activator of epithelial bicarbonate secretion and regulates local and systemic pH balance along with metabolic functions. Its receptor, widely expressed across epithelial and neuroendocrine tissues, enables coordinated responses to digestive phases, systemic alkalosis, and volume regulation. This positions secretin as a corrective hormone of the postprandial alkaline tide and a critical signaling pathway in the prevention of excessive systemic alkalosis. Its signaling intersects with the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, where secretin, angiotensin II, and aldosterone jointly enhance pendrin-mediated chloride reabsorption and bicarbonate secretion during states such as Cl- depletion alkalosis. Conditions with disrupted secretin signaling, most notably cystic fibrosis, demonstrate the physiological importance of secretin-dependent bicarbonate secretion in pancreatic, biliary, renal, and potentially airway epithelia. Overall, secretin emerges not only as a gastrointestinal regulator but also as a central, integrative hormone linking digestion, metabolism, local and systemic acid-base homeostasis, renal electrolyte handling, and systemic volume regulation.

papers.title: Omega-3 fatty acids reprogram tumor-associated macrophage cytokine signaling and suppress pancreatic cancer growth.
papers.abstract: Dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) shape inflammatory signaling within the pancreatic tumor microenvironment (TME), but the cellular mechanisms underlying their effects on tumor progression remain unclear. Using orthotopic models of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), we show that omega-3 (n-3) and omega-6 (n-6) PUFAs are differentially incorporated into tumor lipid pools, generating spatially heterogeneous lipid microenvironments. While an n-6-enriched diet accelerated PDAC growth, an n-3-enriched diet suppressed tumor growth in a T cell-independent manner. Examining inflammatory effects in PDAC tumors, the n-3 PUFA-enriched diet reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 family members, and single-cell and spatial analyses identified tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) as the primary diet-responsive population. Indeed, selective conversion of n-6 to n-3 fatty acids within myeloid cells using an inducible fat-1 transgene, which encodes an n-3 desaturase that converts n-6 to n-3 PUFAs in vivo, was sufficient to suppress tumor growth, whereas fibroblast-restricted conversion had no effect. This finding is the first to formally establish that cellular origin of PUFA metabolism within the TME is a key determinant of tumor progression and identifies TAMs as critical mediators of n-3-dependent tumor suppression. Furthermore, the n-3 PUFA-enriched diet reduced Arg1 + immunosuppressive TAMs and promoted C1q + and MHC-II + antigen-presenting TAM populations enriched for antigen processing machinery and T cell-recruiting chemokines, alongside reduced IL-6 family cytokine production. Together, these findings establish macrophages as key mediators of n-3-driven tumor control and define a mechanism by which dietary lipids remodel cytokine signaling in the PDAC microenvironment.

papers.title: Interventions with mitochondrial-related effects in older adults with type 2 diabetes: Protocol for a systematic review with conditional network meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is central to type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) pathogenesis, driving insulin resistance and pancreatic β-cell dysfunction. Age-related mitochondrial impairment worsens this in older adults, yet evidence on mitochondrial interventions for this group is limited. This protocol outlines a systematic review and conditional network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials evaluating mitochondrial interventions in adults aged 60+ with T2DM. The primary objective of this systematic review and conditional network meta-analysis (NMA) is to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of diverse mitochondrial-related interventions, including pharmacological agents, nutritional supplements, and lifestyle modifications, relative to placebo, standard care, or no intervention, on mitochondrial function biomarkers in adults aged 60 years or older with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Interventions with mitochondrial effects are operationally defined as those whose primary mechanism is known to target mitochondrial pathways or those that are explicitly evaluated for their effects on direct markers of mitochondrial function in the trial. The secondary objectives are: (1) to assess the impact of these interventions on glycemic and metabolic control outcomes including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), fasting insulin, homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), body weight, and body mass index (BMI); (2) to conduct a conditional NMA to compare and rank the relative efficacy of different intervention categories if the evidence network is sufficiently connected and clinically coherent; and (3) to explore potential sources of heterogeneity (e.g., intervention duration, baseline HbA1c levels) via prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses. Prepared per PRISMA-P, the review will follow PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-NMA if applicable. Registered with PROSPERO (ID: CRD420251145356), searches will cover PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to April 2026. Focused on T2DM, mitochondrial function/dysfunction, and interventions, age eligibility will be assessed during full-text screening. Primary analysis includes trials with participants aged 60+ or extractable data for this group; sensitivity analyses will include those with mean/median age ≥ 60. Two reviewers will handle screening, data extraction, and bias assessment using RoB 2.Analysis will focus on trials reporting mitochondrial function outcomes, categorized by biological domain, tissue source, and assay method. Glycemic control, geriatric health, and safety are secondary outcomes. Network meta-analysis will be conducted if a connected evidence network exists; otherwise, pairwise meta-analysis or narrative synthesis will be used. Random-effects models will be employed, with heterogeneity assessed via subgroup analysis and meta-regression. If significant heterogeneity persists, a Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis (SWiM) framework narrative review will be done. Evidence certainty will be appraised using GRADE and CINeMA. Ethics approval is not required for this systematic review as the systematic review will include only previously anonymised data from primary studies. Dissemination of the findings of the final systematic review will occur through publishing in a peer-reviewed journal. PROSPERO registration number CRD420251145356.

papers.title: Design of short-sequenced collagen type III-derived peptides with GPR56 dependent biological activity.
papers.abstract: We have previously shown that activation of G protein-coupled receptor 56 (GPR56) by its endogenous ligand collagen type III (Coll III) improves pancreatic β-cell function and potentiates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS). In the current study, alignment of Coll III and GPR56 genomic DNA revealed three complementary nucleotide regions, enabling the design of three short peptides (NQGCKL.NH2, H.LLSSR.NH2 and NH2.GYYCG.COOH). The peptides in double or triple combinations markedly increased cellular cAMP levels, enhanced GSIS, and improved cell viability both in human (EndoC βH1 cells) and rat pancreatic β-cell lines (INS-1 832/13 cells). These effects were markedly absent in GPR56-knockdown (GPR56-KD) cells, supporting receptor-dependent specificity. The peptide mixtures also counteracted cytokine- and glucotoxicity-induced cellular stress, restoring cAMP generation and insulin secretion. Comparable effects were not observed with dapagliflozin while glibenclamide decreased cell viability under similar conditions. In hepatic cell lines (HepG2, Hep1-6), peptide combinations enhanced cell survival in a GPR56-dependent manner, consistent with a broader role of GPR56 in metabolic regulation. Collectively, the data identify three short sequence collagen III-derived peptides whose biological effects are dependent on GPR56 expression and support their further investigation as tools for studying GPR56-associated cellular signaling for the future in vivo validation.

papers.title: Optimisation and mechanistic characterization of a selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor in pancreatic cancer cells.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a lethal malignancy with limited targeted therapeutic options. Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase kinase 4 (MAP4K4) has been implicated in PDAC progression, but the development of effective MAP4K4 inhibitors requires further improvement in potency, selectivity, and mechanistic characterisation. We previously identified F389-0746 as a selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor with anti-cancer activity in pancreatic cancer. Here, we used the F389-0746 scaffold to guide the selection and evaluation of benzoxazine-based analogs, followed by biochemical, structural, selectivity, and cellular characterisation of the most potent analogue. Among the identified analogs, F389-0736 showed the strongest MAP4K4 inhibitory activity, with an IC 50 value of 44.0 nM, representing an approximately threefold improvement over F389-0746. Docking and structure-activity relationship analyses identified key binding interactions that support the enhanced potency of F389-0736 within the MAP4K4 binding pocket. Kinase profiling further demonstrated the selectivity of F389-0736 for MAP4K4 across the tested kinase panel. CETSA further demonstrated F389-0736-induced thermal stabilisation of MAP4K4, supporting intracellular target engagement. In pancreatic cancer cells, F389-0736 suppressed TAK1, JNK, and p38 phosphorylation and significantly reduced cell viability and proliferation, with IC 50 and GI 50 values of 4.41-4.65 μM and 4.03-5.12 μM, respectively. F389-0736 also inhibited clonogenic growth and induced sub-G1 accumulation with activation of apoptotic signalling. RNA sequencing identified 398 differentially expressed genes and revealed enrichment of inflammatory and stress response pathways, programmed cell death programs, oncogenic signalling perturbation, and metabolic reprogramming. These findings identify F389-0736 as a potent and selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor and support its use as a chemical probe and lead scaffold for investigating MAP4K4-dependent signalling and therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer.

papers.title: CURGET: a combination of common-use polyphenols plus trimetazidine as metabolic therapy for cancer: a theoretical proposal.
papers.abstract: Repurposing inexpensive oral compounds targeting metabolic reprogramming is a pragmatic strategy. CURGET is a five-node oral regimen designed to induce metabolic starvation in tumors. Comprehensive literature search. The malignant phenotype features concurrent upregulation of glycolysis (HK2), glutaminolysis (GLS1), de novo lipogenesis (FASN), the mevalonate pathway (HMGR), and fatty-acid β-oxidation (FAO/3-KAT). CURGET combines four widely available polyphenols and a common cardiac drug: curcumin, urolithin A, resveratrol, EGCG, and trimetazidine to target these five enzymes. Additional mechanisms include context-dependent pro-oxidant activity and epigenetic modulation such as DNMT, HDAC, and HAT inhibition linked to cofactor depletion. This review synthesizes human safety and pharmacokinetic data, plasma AUC overlap with in vitro inhibitory concentrations, knockout evidence of metabolic plasticity, and clinical co-expression of HK2, GLS1, and FASN. CURGET represents a coherent, low-cost oral strategy rather than a finalized protocol. Key priorities include developing bioavailable formulations, conducting preclinical studies with defined metabolic endpoints, and early-phase pharmacokinetic and safety assessments of the combination. If CURGET shows a favorable therapeutic index, it may be most applicable to metabolically characterized tumors, including gastric, pancreatic, and selected breast cancers. Successful development could improve access to affordable metabolic adjuncts and help reduce global disparities in cancer care.

papers.title: Dietary anthocyanins as multifunctional bioactives targeting obesity across experimental and clinical models.
papers.abstract: Obesity has emerged as a critical global health issue, contributing to cardiometabolic and other chronic diseases. Current management strategies, including diet, lifestyle modification, and pharmacotherapy, often lack sustainable efficacy and carry side effects. The search for safe, natural interventions has drawn attention to plant-based bioactives, particularly anthocyanins, which are abundant in dark-pigmented fruits and exhibit antioxidant and anti-obesogenic effects. This review critically evaluates the anti-obesogenic potential of anthocyanins, drawing on in vitro , preclinical, and clinical studies. Preclinical evidence demonstrates that anthocyanins improve lipid and glycemic profiles and insulin sensitivity, while reducing body weight, adiposity, hepatic steatosis, and systemic inflammation. Clinical trials generally support beneficial effects of anthocyanin-rich foods and supplements on selected cardiometabolic parameters ( e.g. , lipids, glycemic control, and inflammation) in individuals with overweight or obesity, while effects on body weight and adiposity are modest or inconsistent. Mechanistically, anthocyanins inhibit pancreatic lipase, adipogenesis, and lipogenesis; promote fatty acid β-oxidation through AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) driven peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) signaling; enhance thermogenesis via upregulation of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) and PR domain-containing 16 (PRDM16); and stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in adipose tissue. In addition, anthocyanins attenuate oxidative stress and chronic inflammation by reducing reactive oxygen species, pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and by modulating nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cell (NF-κB) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways. Furthermore, anthocyanins beneficially modulate the gut microbiota, enriching species such as Akkermansia muciniphila , increasing short-chain fatty acid production, and improving intestinal barrier integrity. Overall, anthocyanins represent a compelling, multi-targeted natural intervention for obesity and its metabolic complications. These natural strategies may complement established pharmacotherapies and, when embedded in plant-forward dietary patterns and sustainable food systems, contribute to a more holistic approach to planetary health.

papers.title: Gut Microbiota and Nutritional Aspects in Pancreatic Diseases: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic diseases, including acute pancreatitis (AP) and chronic pancreatitis (CP), pancreatogenic diabetes mellitus (T3cDM), autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP), and pancreatic cancer (PDAC), are associated with metabolic, inflammatory, and nutritional disturbances. Increasing evidence indicates a bidirectional relationship between pancreatic diseases and the gut microbiota. On the one hand, alterations in microbial composition and function, intestinal barrier dysfunction, and bacterial translocation may contribute to their pathogenesis and progression. On the other hand, pancreatic diseases and associated changes in nutrition and treatment may affect the composition and function of the gut microbiota. This narrative review aimed to discuss the role of the gut microbiota and nutritional aspects in selected pancreatic diseases. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched up to May 2026 for English-language publications, with emphasis on studies from the previous 10 years, while earlier relevant studies were also considered. Google Scholar was used as a supplementary source. Human observational, experimental and mechanistic studies, as well as secondary literature, were considered, addressing pancreatic microbiota, intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, nutrition, and microbiota-targeted interventions. Available evidence indicates that pancreatic diseases are associated with alterations in gut and pancreatic microbial communities, although the reported patterns vary between diseases and studies. These changes may be relevant to intestinal barrier integrity, inflammatory signaling, microbial metabolite production, and, in pancreatic cancer, the tumor microenvironment and treatment response. Nutritional management remains an important component of care, particularly in patients with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and those at risk of malnutrition. However, the causal relationships between pancreatic diseases and microbiota alterations remain incompletely established, and evidence for microbiota-targeted interventions is limited and heterogeneous. Further clinical studies are needed to clarify these interactions and their potential diagnostic and therapeutic relevance.

papers.title: Small-Nerve Fibre Pathology in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease Is Associated with Liver Fat/Inflammation and Improves with Weight Loss.
papers.abstract: Background: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is associated with multiple extrahepatic complications, but its relationship with peripheral neuropathy, even without co-existing type 2 diabetes (T2D), remains poorly understood. Furthermore, to what extent addressing liver and metabolic health would be associated with improvements in small nerve fibre morphology (that mediate neuropathy) is unknown. We investigated the relationship between liver health and small nerve fibre morphology in adults with MASLD before and after diet-induced weight loss and improvements in liver health. Methods: Adults with MASLD (n = 12) and controls without MASLD or T2D (n = 16) underwent anthropometry, biochemistry, transient elastography (TE) and corneal confocal microscopy (CCM). Participants with MASLD then completed a 12-week low-calorie diet (LCD; Counterweight-Plus, ~850 kcal/day) with repeat assessments including multi-organ magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). TE quantified hepatic steatosis (controlled attenuation parameter, CAP), while MRI measured hepatic and pancreatic fat (proton density fat fraction, PDFF) and fibroinflammation (iron-corrected T1, cT1). Neuropathy was assessed using validated questionnaires and CCM-derived corneal nerve fibre density (CNFD), branch density (CNBD) and fibre length (CNFL). The primary outcome measure was change in liver PDFF. Associations between hepatic and neuropathy measures were assessed using correlation and multivariable linear regression. Results: Compared with controls, MASLD participants had higher liver fat and metabolic dysfunction, with reduced CNFD (25.7 vs. 28.4 fibres/mm 2 , p = 0.03) and CNFL (14.1 vs. 17.1 mm/mm 2 , p = 0.02). In multivariable regression, TE-derived CAP was independently associated with CNFD (β -0.03 (95% CI -0.06, -0.01), p < 0.05), while total cholesterol was associated with CNFL (β -1.54 (95% CI -2.81, -0.27), p < 0.02). After LCD, participants lost 12.5 kg with reductions in metabolic syndrome components ( p = 0.04) and liver fat (ΔPDFF -5.0%, p = 0.03). Neuropathic symptoms improved and CNFD increased (+1.87 fibres/mm 2 , p = 0.05). Reduction in liver fat correlated with increased CNFL (r = -0.63, p = 0.03), while change in hepatic fibroinflammation (ΔcT1) correlated with neuropathy disability (r = 0.62, p = 0.04) and small-fibre symptom scores (r = 0.47, p = 0.05). Conclusions: These exploratory findings suggest that MASLD, even without T2D, may be associated with small nerve fibre abnormalities and neuropathic symptoms. Diet-induced weight loss improved liver, metabolic and neural health in parallel. Larger prospective confirmatory studies are required to more precisely establish this relationship both at baseline and with interventions.

papers.title: From Genes to Diets: A Critical Review of Genetic, Nutrigenomic and Epigenetic Mechanisms in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) represents over 90% of diabetes cases globally, posing a growing public health crisis with an estimated 783 million adults projected to be affected by 2045. This condition arises from a complex interplay of insulin resistance, progressive pancreatic β-cell dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation, strongly influenced by genetic predisposition, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and poor dietary habits. While genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified key susceptibility loci, including TCF7L2 , PPARG , and KCNJ11 , these varian0ts explain only ~10% of T2D heritability, underscoring the critical role of gene-environment interactions. This review synthesizes current evidence on the genetic, nutrigenomic, and epigenetic mechanisms underlying T2D pathogenesis and progression. We examine how dietary components, such as flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids, and bioactive compounds from natural products, modulate gene expression via transcription factors and influence insulin sensitivity, oxidative stress, and inflammation. Furthermore, we explore the emerging role of epigenetic modifications, including DNA methylation, histone acetylation, and chromatin remodeling, in mediating the lasting effects of hyperglycemia and environmental factors on T2D risk. The potential of epigenetic biomarkers for early diagnosis, patient stratification, and personalized therapy is discussed. Finally, we highlight how next-generation sequencing and artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning and deep learning models, are advancing multi-omics data integration, enabling improved T2D subtype classification, prognosis prediction, and the development of precision nutrition and pharmacoepigenetic strategies.

papers.title: A Retrospective Analysis of the Association Between Prediabetes and Biomarkers of Intestinal Permeability in Patients with Prediabetes from Durban, South Africa.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a metabolic disorder characterized by insufficient insulin production and diminished insulin receptor sensitivity. Prediabetes, which often precedes T2DM, involves elevated blood glucose levels that do not yet meet T2DM diagnostic criteria. Research has shown that complications linked to T2DM often begin during this prediabetic phase. In this study, we examined changes in intestinal barrier integrity during prediabetes by measuring biomarkers associated with intestinal permeability. With ethical approval, samples were collected from King Edward Hospital and Albert Luthuli Central Hospital in Durban and categorized into type 2 diabetes (T2D), prediabetes (PD), and non-prediabetes (NPD) groups. Blood levels of neutrophils and HbA1c were measured and analyzed, followed by serum zonulin and plasma levels of markers, including IFABP, sCD14, TNF-α, IL-6, glucose, insulin, and pancreatic lipase, which were measured and analyzed. The results showed significantly higher levels of these markers in the PD group compared to the NPD group, with further elevations in the T2D group. These findings align with existing research suggesting an association between increased intestinal permeability and the development of prediabetes. Altogether, these results indicate that prediabetes is a transitional phase marked by metabolic and intestinal permeability changes, though less severe than in T2DM. This underscores the need for additional research to cover a wider range of metabolic health, oxidative stress, inflammation, and vascular function markers, as such comprehensive assessments could provide deeper insight into underlying physiological processes.

papers.title: Gjb2 V37M Modifies Metabolic Responses to Chronic High-Fat Feeding in Mice.
papers.abstract: GJB2 encodes connexin 26 (Cx26), and pathogenic GJB2 variants are among the most common genetic causes of hereditary hearing loss; because Cx26 is expressed in metabolically relevant tissues including liver, pancreas, and adipose tissue, whether the hearing-loss-associated c.109G>A (p.V37M) variant also modifies systemic metabolic responses to high-fat diet (HFD) exposure remains unclear. Three-month-old male wild-type (WT) and homozygous Gjb2 V37M mice were assigned to low-fat diet (LFD) or high-fat diet (HFD) groups, generating four study groups: WT-LFD, WT-HFD, V37M-LFD, and V37M-HFD. The mice were followed until 12 months of age, with dietary intervention continued for 9 months. Body weight, body mass index (BMI), fasting blood glucose, serum triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol were assessed at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. An oral glucose tolerance test was performed at 9 months, and omental fat was measured at 12 months. WT-HFD mice showed marked progressive increases in body weight and BMI, whereas increases were less pronounced in V37M-HFD mice. At 12 months, body weight and BMI did not differ significantly between V37M-LFD and V37M-HFD mice. Fasting glucose, glucose tolerance, triglyceride, and HDL cholesterol profiles differed among groups. Omental fat weight also differed significantly, although the only significant post hoc comparison was between WT-HFD and V37M-LFD mice. These findings indicate that Gjb2 V37M is associated with distinct weight, glycemic, and lipid responses during chronic dietary exposure, suggesting that GJB2 variants may modify systemic metabolic adaptation to chronic high-fat feeding.

papers.title: The Klf7/Glut2/Ins2 Axis Regulates Glucose Homeostasis.
papers.abstract: Krüppel-like factor 7 ( KLF7 ) is a Cys 2 /His 2 zinc-finger transcription factor implicated in metabolic regulation. Although KLF7 variants are associated with type 2 diabetes (T2D), its role in β-cell glucose homeostasis remains unclear. Klf7 is downregulated in β-cells from mice and humans with established diabetes, and high glucose directly suppresses Klf7 expression in isolated islets. β-cell-specific Klf7 knockout (β-KLF7KO) and overexpression (β-KLF7OE) mouse models were generated, along with AAV-mediated rescue models. Islet transcriptomics, glucose-stimulated insulin secretion assays, luciferase reporter assays, and lentiviral knockdown/overexpression in INS1 and 1.1B4 cells were performed. Here we show that KLF7 is downregulated in β-cells from diabetic human donors and mice. β-cell-specific deletion of Klf7 in mice impaired insulin secretion and glucose tolerance, accompanied by a 47% reduction in Slc2a2 ( Glut2 ) expression. Klf7 overexpression in vitro suppressed insulin secretion, revealing opposing transcriptional regulation of Glut2 and Ins2 . Luciferase reporter assays confirmed that Klf7 directly activates the Glut2 promoter and represses the Ins2 promoter, establishing an opposing transcriptional regulatory mechanism. This regulatory mechanism is conserved in the 1.1B4 human pancreatic islet fusion cell line, in which KLF7 knockdown derepressed INS and suppressed GLUT2 expression. AAV-mediated restoration of either Klf7 or Glut2 in β-KLF7KO mice largely rescued the metabolic defects, identifying Glut2 as a principal downstream mediator. Given that KLF7 declines under hyperglycaemic stress and its loss is sufficient to impair β-cell function, the Klf7/Glut2/Ins2 axis may represent an early, targetable step in β-cell dysfunction; whether KLF7 decline precedes the onset of glucose intolerance in a natural progression model remains to be determined by longitudinal studies.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Dynamics in Diabetes Mellitus and Its Complications: Mechanisms, Pathological Roles, and Therapeutic Implications.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a progressive metabolic disorder in which mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a central contributor to metabolic deterioration and diabetic complications. However, whether dysregulated mitochondrial dynamics represents a primary pathogenic driver, an adaptive response, or a consequence of metabolic stress remains incompletely understood. This review summarizes current advances in the molecular mechanisms governing mitochondrial fission, fusion, and mitophagy, with particular emphasis on their coordinated roles in mitochondrial quality control rather than isolated morphological changes. We discuss how disrupted mitochondrial dynamics contributes to pancreatic β-cell dysfunction, insulin resistance, diabetic nephropathy (DN), diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and diabetic osteoporosis (DOP) through context-dependent regulation of oxidative stress, bioenergetics, inflammation, and endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria crosstalk. Furthermore, we critically evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies, including metformin, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, mitochondrial fission inhibitors, and mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, highlighting both their therapeutic potential and current translational challenges. We propose that restoring the physiological equilibrium among mitochondrial fission, fusion, and mitophagy, rather than unidirectionally inhibiting a single pathway, represents a more promising strategy for preventing and treating diabetes and its complications.

papers.title: Age-Related Variation in Flavonoid Composition, Human Pancreatic Lipase Inhibition, and Preliminary Brine Shrimp Lethality of Rhododendron adamsii Leaves and Sagan Dali Tea.
papers.abstract: Rhododendron adamsii Rehder is an important Asian ericaceous species widely used throughout the region as a food plant for producing sagan dali tea. Although the leaves of R. adamsii are consumed at different developmental stages, potential variations in their metabolite composition and bioactivity have not yet been scientifically investigated. To address this knowledge gap, first-year, second-year, and litterfall leaves of R. adamsii , together with sagan dali tea decoctions, were subjected to LC-MS profiling and quantification, in vitro assays measuring human pancreatic lipase (hPL) inhibition, and toxicity evaluation using the brine shrimp lethality (BSL) assay. The results showed that leaf age significantly affects ( p < 0.05) phenolic diversity, total content, and antilipase activity in sagan dali tea, establishing the following performance ranking: first-year > second-year > litterfall. Leaf senescence caused a decrease or disappearance of flavonoid glycosides, accompanied by an increase in free aglycones, ultimately altering the tea's chemical composition. Specifically, the predominant compounds in first-year leaves were myricetin 3'- O -xylopyranoside (881-917 mg/100 g) and quercetin 3- O -galactoside (672-714 mg/100 g), whereas free myricetin (427-451 mg/100 g) predominated in the litterfall. The highest antilipase potency of sagan dali tea was recorded in first-year leaves (IC 50 30.65-33.47 μg/mL vs. orlistat 35.28 μg/mL). This activity was associated with the presence of myricetin, quercetin, and gossypetin in both free and glycosylated forms, with IC 50 values lower than that of orlistat under the tested conditions. Furthermore, the BSL assay showed LC 50 values > 1000 μg/mL, indicating low lethality of sagan dali tea to brine shrimp across all categories under the tested conditions. However, these results provide only preliminary information and do not establish food or human safety. In summary, the age of R. adamsii leaves is a critical parameter determining phytocomponent concentrations and associated bioactivity while consistently maintaining low brine shrimp lethality under the tested conditions. These findings provide a biochemical basis for further research into the optimal use of R. adamsii leaf material.

papers.title: Rewiring Biological Barriers in Pancreatic Diseases with Metal-Organic Frameworks.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic diseases, particularly pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), remain among the most challenging disorders to diagnose and treat owing to a series of interconnected biological barriers, including dense stromal desmoplasia, profound immunosuppression, hypoxia, therapeutic resistance, and the lack of effective early-detection strategies. Overcoming these barriers requires multifunctional platforms capable of integrating diagnosis, microenvironment regulation, and precision therapy within a single system. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), a class of highly tunable porous crystalline materials, have emerged as uniquely suited candidates for this purpose because of their programmable composition, structural versatility, catalytic activity, and capacity for multifunctional integration. Notably, MOFs have evolved from passive drug carriers into active regulators of disease-associated biological processes, enabling enhanced drug delivery, extracellular matrix remodeling, ferroptosis- and cuproptosis-based precision therapy, energy-triggered reactive oxygen species generation, immune microenvironment reprogramming, and imaging-guided theranostics. Beyond pancreatic cancer, emerging evidence further supports their potential applications in pancreatitis management and interventional therapeutic enhancement. In this review, we systematically summarize recent advances in the rational engineering of MOFs for pancreatic diseases, focusing on how material design strategies are leveraged to overcome key pathological barriers and improve therapeutic outcomes. We further discuss current challenges associated with biosafety, biodegradation, large-scale manufacturing, and clinical translation, while highlighting future opportunities for the development of next-generation MOF-based precision nanomedicines. By integrating advances across materials science, nanomedicine, and pancreatic disease biology, this review provides a comprehensive framework for the design and translational development of MOF-enabled diagnostic and therapeutic platforms.

papers.title: Targeting SERPINB5 and MSLN for Pancreatic Cancer Therapy.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives : Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States and lacks efficient therapeutic options. Serine peptidase inhibitor, clade B, member 5 (SERPINB5) is non-inhibitory toward serine proteases, yet it has diverse biological functions, including regulating cell migration, cell death, gene expression, and stress responses. Mesothelin (MSLN) is a tumor-associated antigen that is broadly overexpressed on various malignant tumor cells and plays a crucial role in promoting proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. Methods : We integrated public database analyses, cell-line screening, gene knockdown and overexpression, immunoblotting, cell viability and apoptosis assays, flow cytometry, chromatin immunoprecipitation paired with quantitative PCR (ChIP-qPCR), and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy to investigate SERPINB5 and MSLN functions, developing a novel and effective therapeutic strategy for patients with pancreatic cancer. Results : Both SERPINB5 and MSLN are highly expressed and negatively associated with the overall survival of PC patients. Our mechanistic study suggests that SERPINB5 negatively regulates the mitochondrial protein dehydrogenase/reductase 2 (DHRS2) to promote PC cell survival; consequently, SERPINB5 depletion induces PC cell apoptosis. Of note, SERPINB5 depletion increases MSLN transcription by enhancing c-Myc binding to the MSLN promoter region, which in turn suppresses the mitochondrial protein DHRS2 and leads to resistance to apoptosis in PC cells. Our genetic ablation study shows that SERPINB5 and MSLN are critical for PC cell survival, and that depleting both proteins synergistically induces PC cell apoptosis. Gemcitabine (GEM) is a standard chemotherapy drug for PC treatment. Our study shows that SERPINB5-high PC cells display greater sensitivity to GEM than SERPINB5-low PC cells. GEM treatment increases mitochondrial DHRS2 protein expression, similar to the effect of SERPINB5 knockdown, whereas upregulated MSLN confers apoptotic resistance by decreasing DHRS2 levels. Conclusions : Our in vitro study demonstrates that sequential treatment with GEM followed by anti-MSLN chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells is an effective and promising strategy for patients with pancreatic cancer. Future studies using mouse models may validate the efficacy of this sequential treatment strategy in vivo.

papers.title: Potential Physiological Convergence Between GLP-1 Receptor Signaling and Hepatocyte TAZ in Metabolic Liver Disease: From Metabolic Homeostasis to Fibrotic Remodeling.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) progresses when nutrient excess, insulin resistance, adipose dysfunction, and hepatocellular stress overwhelm hepatic adaptation. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) improve weight, glycemic control, and steatohepatitis, and semaglutide has demonstrated histological improvement in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). In parallel, the transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ; WWTR1) has emerged as a nutrient-, cholesterol-, and mechanics-responsive regulator linking stressed hepatocytes to inflammation and fibrogenesis through Hippo-YAP/TAZ signaling and Indian hedgehog. This narrative review integrates incretin physiology with cell-specific TAZ biology across the gut-brain-axis, adipose tissue, pancreatic islets, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, hepatocytes, immune cells, and hepatic stellate cells. Recent evidence that semaglutide can signal through intrahepatic sinusoidal endothelial GLP-1 receptors provides a weight-loss-independent route to reduced hepatic inflammation and fibrosis; however, it does not establish that TAZ is a downstream mediator. The evidence therefore supports a multilevel convergence model in which GLP-1RAs lower metabolic and inflammatory inputs that favor TAZ activation, while direct GLP-1RA-to-TAZ signaling remains a testable hypothesis. Receptor-validated, cell-specific, weight-controlled, and longitudinal human studies are needed to distinguish mediation from parallel response and to determine whether TAZ-pathway biomarkers can guide mechanism-based therapy.
keywords: Transcriptional Coactivator with PDZ-Binding Motif Proteins

papers.title: TRPs-NCX2 Axis Jointly Preserves Pancreatic Beta Cell Susceptibility/Sensitivity to Elevated Glucose.
papers.abstract: Background: For appropriate glucose sensing, pancreatic beta-cells essentially establish a constant mitochondria-directed endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca 2+ leak via phosphorylated presenilin-1 (PS1). In the current work, we investigated how cells maintain the ER Ca 2+ content during this continuous Ca 2+ leak. Methods: Ca 2+ imaging for ER, cytosolic and subplasmalemmal Ca 2+ , high resolution respirometry, and ELISA for insulin secretion were used. Results: A novel ER Ca 2+ refilling mechanism driven by reverse-mode NCX2, which is fueled by local Na + influxes through TRPC3 and TRPV4 channels that are independent of STIM-ORAI1 was found in pancreatic rodent and human beta cell lines. Disrupting this TRPs-NCX2 axis reduces subplasmalemmal Ca 2+ levels, abolishes glucose-induced cytosolic Ca 2+ oscillations, suppresses glucose-triggered elevation in mitochondrial energetics, and impairs first-phase insulin secretion. Conclusions: We identified a novel, ORAI1-independent "TRPs-NCX2" relay that couples Na + influx via TRPC3 and TRPV4 to NCX2 reverse mode to maintain ER Ca 2+ stores during physiological basal ER Ca 2+ leakage, which is fundamental to beta-cell responsiveness to elevated glucose.

papers.title: Mitochondria-Endoplasmic Reticulum Crosstalk in Pancreatic β-Cell Stress: A Driver of Diabetes.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic β-cell failure is central to the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes (T2D), developing when chronic metabolic stress overwhelms the adaptive capacity of these cells. Because insulin biosynthesis and glucose-stimulated secretion depend on tightly coordinated organelle function, crosstalk between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria strongly influences β-cell fate. The two organelles are physically coupled at mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs), contact sites that synchronize ER Ca 2+ release with mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, and that help regulate redox balance, autophagy, mitophagy and the unfolded protein response. This review draws together evidence on three questions. First, which stresses converge on the β-cell: ER stress, oxidative stress and dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy. Second, how ER-mitochondria crosstalk sustains β-cell health through Ca 2+ handling and the proteins that maintain MAM integrity, including inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP 3 ) receptors, voltage-dependent anion channel 1 (VDAC1), mitofusin 2 (Mfn2) and the ER stress sensors IRE1α and PERK. Third, how glucolipotoxic and inflammatory stress remodels these contacts and pushes communication towards a maladaptive state marked by mitochondrial Ca 2+ overload, ROS accumulation, defective organelle quality control, cellular senescence and apoptosis. We contrast rodent and human data, where MAM composition and glucotoxic responses diverge, and consider therapeutic strategies, such as incretin-based agents and the mitochondrial-derived peptide MOTS-c, that target this interface to preserve β-cell function in diabetes.

papers.title: Aldehyde Dehydrogenase 2 Activity Assessed Using the Acetaldehyde Breath Test Is Associated with Benign Pancreatic Disease and Pancreatic Cancer: A Case-Control Study.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) detoxifies acetaldehyde, and impaired ALDH2 activity has been implicated in carcinogenesis. The acetaldehyde breath test (ABT) enables noninvasive functional assessment of ALDH2 activity, but its association with pancreatic disease remains unclear. We examined associations between ABT-assessed ALDH2 activity and pancreatic disease outcomes. Methods: This case-control study included 287 health checkup participants, 131 patients with benign pancreatic disease, and 65 patients with pancreatic cancer. Participants underwent ABT, and the acetaldehyde-to-ethanol (A/E) ratio was calculated. The ALDH2 inactive phenotype was defined as an A/E ratio ≥ 23.3. Multinomial logistic regression used health checkup participants as the reference. Results: The median A/E ratio was higher in patients with benign pancreatic disease and pancreatic cancer than in health checkup participants (21.7 and 24.2 vs. 13.6; p < 0.001). The ALDH2 inactive phenotype was associated with benign pancreatic disease (relative risk ratio [RRR], 3.55; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.85-6.83) and pancreatic cancer (RRR, 4.82; 95% CI, 2.13-10.88). The highest A/E ratio category was also associated with benign pancreatic disease (RRR, 8.77; 95% CI, 3.59-21.39) and pancreatic cancer (RRR, 12.79; 95% CI, 4.41-37.09). Exploratory spline analyses showed associations between higher A/E ratios and pancreatic disease outcomes without clear evidence of nonlinearity. Conclusions: A higher ABT-derived A/E ratio was associated with benign pancreatic disease and pancreatic cancer in this selected case-control study. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether functional assessment of aldehyde metabolism provides clinically useful information for pancreatic disease risk assessment. Trial registration number: UMIN Clinical Trials Registry (UMIN-CTR), UMIN000052609; registered 1 November 2023.

papers.title: Revisiting chronic pancreatitis as a risk factor for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: toward precision risk stratification.
papers.abstract: Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is an established risk factor for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). However, individual risk varies substantially, and the association between CP and PDAC is more complex than a uniform inflammation-driven pathway. Reverse causation, shared etiological factors, and biological heterogeneity may contribute to the observed association. We critically review epidemiological, mechanistic, and causal evidence linking CP with PDAC, focusing on heterogeneity across CP subtypes and disease trajectories. We examine five domains potentially relevant to individual PDAC risk: genetic susceptibility, cumulative pancreatic injury, metabolic trajectories including new-onset diabetes, longitudinal imaging phenotypes, and emerging molecular alterations. We propose a multidomain framework for individualized and dynamic risk stratification and risk-adapted surveillance. CP should not be regarded as a uniformly high-risk condition for PDAC. Individual risk is shaped by the interaction of genetic, inflammatory, metabolic, structural, and molecular factors. The key question should therefore shift from whether CP increases PDAC risk to which patients are most likely to develop clinically consequential PDAC. Although multidomain and longitudinal assessment may enable targeted surveillance, most biomarkers and prediction strategies remain insufficiently validated. Prospective studies are required to determine whether this approach improves early detection and patient outcomes.

papers.title: Impaired insulin secretion in response to mixed meal ingestion is associated with hypersomatostatinemia in individuals with cystic fibrosis.
papers.abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a monogenic disease characterized by exocrine pancreas insufficiency, glucose intolerance, and a high prevalence of diabetes. Diminished insulin secretion is a key contributor to glucose intolerance and diabetes in people with CF, yet the pathophysiology of this deficiency is not fully understood. Somatostatin is a hormone secreted by several tissues in the body, including the delta cells of the pancreas, and is known to inhibit insulin secretion; however, its role in postprandial hypoinsulinemia in people with CF remains unclear. This cross-sectional study included 16 people with CF (CF group) and 8 healthy control subjects (HC), each of whom underwent a mixed meal tolerance test, during which their glucoregulatory responses were assessed. We hypothesized that impaired insulin secretion in CF would be associated with hypersomatostatinemia. Plasma glucose responses to the mixed meal were higher in CF compared to HC (AUC of 27,656±2,215 and 20,564±1,028 mg/dL*180 min, respectively, p<0.05), whereas the AUC for insulin (5866±730 and 11090±1628 µU/mL*180 min, respectively; p<0.05), and C-peptide (608±42 and 998±127 pg/mL*180 min, respectively; p<0.05), were both lower. Hypersomatostatinemia in CF (AUC of 4682±278 and 3353±277 pg/mL*180 min in CF and HC, respectively, p<0.01), was inversely associated with C-peptide (r=-0.54; p<0.01), and insulin (r=-0.60; p<0.01) responses to the mixed meal. These data suggest that hypersomatostatinemia is associated with diminished insulin secretion in people with CF, and that it could be a target for improving glucose tolerance in this population.

papers.title: A coordinated paracrine islet cell network regulating β-cell Ca 2+ dynamics.
papers.abstract: Pulsatile insulin secretion originates from oscillations in cytosolic free Ca 2+ in pancreatic islet β-cells. Decades of work have identified multiple determinants of these oscillations, including glucose metabolism, ion channels, ER Ca 2+ handling, cellular heterogeneity, and paracrine and neurohormonal signaling. Yet their relative contributions under physiological conditions remain unresolved because each experimental preparation preserves only a subset of these regulatory layers. Here, we review evidence that intercellular paracrine signaling, in addition to cell-autonomous β-cell machinery, is an important determinant of oscillation frequency and coordination. Simultaneous Ca 2+ imaging of α-cells and β-cells reveals tightly coordinated activity, with α-cells following β-cells after a conserved ∼20-s delay. Perturbation of glucagon signaling further indicates that α-cell signaling can modulate β-cell oscillation frequency. Complementing these findings, in vivo imaging of islets engrafted in the anterior chamber of the eye shows that α-cell expansion enhances β-cell Ca 2+ coordination in a glucagon-receptor-dependent manner. Extending this circuit to δ-cells, somatostatin limits oscillation frequency primarily by suppressing α-cell glucagon release, thereby enabling the δ-cell-α-cell-β-cell paracrine circuit to shift β-cell oscillations between fast, mixed, and slow regimes. Importantly, a glycemia-dependent slow-to-fast transition is lost in diabetic mice and rescued by GLP-1 receptor agonism. Under anesthesia-free conditions, however, islets in awake animals occupy a slow, highly synchronized oscillatory regime in which glucose modulates amplitude, period, and plateau fraction without altering network coordination. Together, these findings suggest that the δ-cell-α-cell-β-cell circuit represents an important regulatory layer shaping β-cell Ca 2+ oscillations alongside intrinsic β-cell mechanisms and extrinsic physiological inputs. β-cell dysfunction may therefore involve not only altered oscillation frequency and coordination, but also disrupted paracrine regulation by glucagon and somatostatin.

papers.title: Pancreatic cancer cell and stellate cell-derived exosome crosstalk mediates pancreatic cancer-related diabetes.
papers.abstract: Diabetes is a known risk factor, and a distinct form termed pancreatic cancer-related diabetes (PCRD) often precedes the diagnosis of cancer by 3-5 years, offering a potential window for intervention. We hypothesised that interactions between stromal pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) and cancer cells trigger secretion of exosomal factors that impair islet function and insulin signalling, contributing to PCRD pathogenesis. KC (KrasLSL-G12D/+; Pdx1-Cre) mice were fed a high-fructose diet (HFrD) or control diet for 16 weeks. Exosomes were isolated from monocultures and co-cultures of cancer/PanIN cells with PSCs, characterised by nanoparticle tracking analysis and transmission electron microscopy, and incubated with mouse β-cells (MIN6) and peripheral cells (hepatocytes, adipocytes, skeletal myocytes). Effects on insulin secretion and insulin-signalling factors were examined. Exosomal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) expression was modulated by siRNA to assess functional impact. HFrD induced marked glucose intolerance in KC mice and was accompanied by enhanced PSC activation, macrophage infiltration, inflammation, and accelerated PanIN progression. Exosomes from PSCs, cancer cells, and co-cultures displayed typical morphology and marker expression and were efficiently internalised by β-cells and hepatocytes. Functionally, exosomes significantly impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in mouse and human β-cells without altering insulin content. In hepatocytes, PSC-, cancer-, and co-culture-derived exosomes reduced key insulin-signalling components, including IR, IRS, AKT, FOXO1 and GLUT2, and inhibited glucose uptake. Silencing exosomal G6PD partially restored hepatocyte insulin signalling. This study identifies a potential contributor to PCRD and suggests a possible mechanistic role for exosomal G6PD in impaired insulin signalling associated with PCRD.

papers.title: Nutritional and physiological response to feed form and sodium bicarbonate-adjusted dietary electrolyte balance in lactating sows under heat stress.
papers.abstract: Heat stress (HS) during lactation poses a critical challenge in swine production, often impairing feed intake, metabolic function, and reproductive performance in sows. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of feed form (mash vs. pellet) and dietary electrolyte balance (dEB; 230 vs. 290 mEq/kg) adjusted with sodium bicarbonate on sow performance, litter growth, immune response, antioxidant status, and gut microbiota under HS conditions. A total of 40 multiparous sows were assigned to four treatments in a 2 × 2 factorial design: Mlow (mash + 230 mEq/kg), Mhigh (mash + 290 mEq/kg), Plow (pellet + 230 mEq/kg), and Phigh (pellet + 290 mEq/kg). Each treatment contained 10 sows with 3-5 parity and their initial body weight was 241.83 ± 16 kg at d 112 of lactation. The trial spanned from parturition to weaning (21 days) during summer at an average temperature of 28.8°C. Results showed that sows fed pelleted diets (Plow, Phigh) and higher dEB levels (Mhigh, Phigh) had higher ( p < 0.001) average daily feed intake. Piglets from Mhigh and Phigh sows had increased ( p = 0.001) weaning weights. Dry matter digestibility was increased ( p = 0.022) in sows receiving pelleted diets. The tumour necrosis factor-alpha was lower ( p < 0.001) in Plow, Phigh, and Mhigh ( p = 0.010), with an interaction ( p = 0.013) in feed forms and dEB. The interleukin-1β was lower ( p < 0.001) in Plow and Phigh, with higher ( p < 0.001) superoxide dismutase activity in Phigh and Plow. Hair cortisol was lower ( p = 0.048) in pelleted groups, suggesting lower physiological stress. Although alpha diversity did not differ, beta diversity and relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Turicibacter indicated microbial shifts influenced by feed form. In conclusion, pelleted feed form and higher dEB, particularly the Phigh treatment, enhanced feed intake, litter performance, and anti-inflammatory status without negatively affecting milk composition or gut integrity. These findings support the integration of feed form and electrolyte strategies to improve sow productivity under HS conditions.

papers.title: Enhancing canine intestinal health: evodiamine-enriched functional diet modulates microbiota and metabolic pathways.
papers.abstract: This study investigated the effects of an evodiamine (EVO)-enriched functional diet on canine intestinal health, with a focus on its modulation of microbiota composition and promotion of intestinal well-being. After a one-week acclimatization period, dogs were randomly assigned to either the control group or the EVO group, receiving their respective diets for 8 weeks. Physiological and hematological parameters were assessed at 0, 4, and 8 weeks, and fresh feces were collected at 4 and 8 weeks for microbial analysis to evaluate the impact of the functional diet on canine intestinal microorganisms. The 8-week trial revealed that the functional gut diet regulated microbial composition, improving intestinal health without affecting body metrics or routine blood indicators, and the diet's safety was affirmed by normal biochemical indices. Comparative analysis indicated altered microbial abundance in model dogs, highlighting positive changes favoring intestinal barrier enhancement. Alpha diversity analysis confirmed increased species diversity in the EVO group, reflecting a healthier gut. Moreover, the study demonstrated the functional diet's regulatory impact on microbial metabolic pathways and species differences without observed side effects, reinforcing its positive influence on gut health. Therefore, the canine intestinal functional diet containing EVO showed no significant impact on physiological health but exhibited regulatory effects on intestinal microorganisms. EVO effectively modulated microbial abundance and diversity, fostering intestinal mucosal repair and barrier protection. Additionally, the diet improved microbial function by regulating canine intestinal metabolic pathways. This study serves as a valuable reference for future research in promoting canine intestinal health.

papers.title: Gut microbiota in esophageal cancer: mechanisms, clinical implications, and therapeutic potential.
papers.abstract: Esophageal cancer (EC) is a highly prevalent and aggressive gastrointestinal malignancy. Late diagnosis and heterogeneous responses to chemoradiotherapy and immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapies severely challenge clinical management. Accumulating evidence suggests that gut microbiota dysbiosis influences esophageal mucosal malignant transformation, tumor progression, and therapeutic outcomes through the gut-esophageal axis. However, most existing research remains correlational. To bridge this gap, this review critically synthesizes the dysbiosis signatures of EC and establishes a five-tier evidence grading framework to rigorously distinguish causal mechanisms from preclinical inferences. This microbial regulation is predominantly driven by metabolite-mediated signaling, remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment (TME), intestinal barrier disruption, and oncogenic pathway activation. We functionally classify EC-associated dysbiosis into pro-tumorigenic, anti-tumorigenic, and context-dependent taxa, emphasizing a multidimensional ecosystem perspective. Furthermore, we evaluate the utility of gut microbial signatures as predictive biomarkers for neoadjuvant therapy and prognosis. Microbiota-targeted intervention strategies, including fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), microecological preparations, and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), have entered clinical exploration as adjunctive approaches to optimize treatment efficacy. Finally, we address current translational barriers and propose future directions, emphasizing multi-omics integration, spatial transcriptomics, and artificial intelligence (AI). This provides an objective, mechanistically grounded framework for advancing microbiota-guided personalized oncology in EC.

papers.title: Exploratory assessment of N-carbamylglutamate supplementation on feed efficiency and protein utilization in early growing pigs fed low crude protein diet.
papers.abstract: Reducing dietary crude protein (CP) levels while supplementing with essential amino acids (AA) has been widely studied as a strategy to maintain nutrient balance while lowering nitrogen excretion. Among feed additives, N-carbamylglutamate (NCG), an arginine precursor with superior stability and mitochondrial permeability, has emerged as a promising feed additive for improving intestinal development and overall pig performance. A total of 240 crossbred grower pigs were allotted to four dietary treatments based on initial body weight. Treatments were arranged in a 2 × 2 factorial design with two levels of dietary CP (MCP, 16% moderate CP; LCP, 14% low CP) and two levels of NCG supplementation (without NCG [WN]; NS, 0.1% NCG supplementation). Each treatment had 10 replicates, with six (3 male and 3 female) pigs per pen, and the feeding trial lasted for 4 weeks. Pigs fed the MCP diet tended to have higher final BW ( p = 0.088) compared with the LCP diet. Feed efficiency was greater in MCP than LCP ( p < 0.05) and also tended to be enhanced in the NS ( p = 0.089). CP digestibility tended to increase in the NS group compared with the WN ( p = 0.093). The digestibility of arginine and tyrosine was increased in the NS group compared with the WN group ( p < 0.05). Furthermore, lysine ( p = 0.067), glycine ( p = 0.058), and the average of essential AA ( p = 0.091) digestibility tended to be increased in the NS. The NS group showed higher concentrations of arginine, lysine, essential AA, non-essential AA, and total AA in the blood ( p < 0.05). Trypsin activity showed a tendency to increase in the NS group compared with the WN group ( p = 0.087). In conclusion, dietary NCG supplementation in a low-protein diet showed potential to improve feed efficiency, AA digestibility, and serum AA profiles in early growing pigs.

papers.title: Nutritional support in bone infections: mechanisms, strategies, and clinical practice.
papers.abstract: Bone infections, including osteomyelitis and periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), are characterized by prolonged treatment, high recurrence, and functional impairment. Persistent inflammation induces hypercatabolism, negative nitrogen balance, and micronutrient depletion, impairing immune defense and bone repair. Systematic nutritional assessment remains insufficient. This review elucidates metabolic mechanisms under infectious stress, evaluates macronutrients, micronutrients, and immunomodulatory nutrients in infection control and bone regeneration, and proposes a clinical nutritional management framework. A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and CNKI from January 2020 to April 2026 to inform this narrative review. Studies on metabolic profiles, nutritional interventions, or nutritional status-outcome associations in osteomyelitis or PJI were included. Data were synthesized across five dimensions: molecular mechanisms, macronutrient therapy, micronutrient functions, immunonutrition, and implementation pathways, with evidence graded by OCEBM levels. TNF-α and IL-6 drive muscle degradation via ubiquitin-proteasome activation and mTORC1 suppression, causing negative nitrogen balance; zinc, selenium, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are depleted. Nutritional risk markers (albumin ≤ 3.5 g/dl and/or lymphocytes ≤ 1.5 × 10 3 /μl) are associated with 2--4-fold higher risks of postoperative infection, wound dehiscence, and sepsis, and increased 2-year osteomyelitis risk (RR = 2.55). Protein (1.5-2.0 g/kg/d) and energy (25-35 kcal/kg/d) correct nitrogen balance and support immunity and bone repair. Vitamin D induces cathelicidin via VDR, exerting mineralization and anti-infection effects; zinc/selenium alleviate oxidative damage; omega-3 PUFAs provide anti-inflammatory effects. Probiotics show gut-bone axis potential with limited evidence. High-quality RCTs for bone infections are lacking; most recommendations derive from observational studies (evidence levels C-D). Nutritional support should be elevated to core status. We recommend routine albumin, prealbumin, and lymphocyte screening, and a "screening → assessment → stratified intervention → dynamic monitoring" pathway. Enteral nutrition is preferred perioperatively, with 1.5-2.0 g/kg/d protein and 25-35 kcal/kg/d energy, plus individualized correction of vitamin D, zinc, and selenium deficiencies. Multicenter RCTs are needed to validate immunonutrient efficacy and advance precision nutrition via metabolomics and gut-bone axis mechanisms.

papers.title: Endocrine determinants of MASLD: mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately 30% of adults worldwide, yet is still framed largely as a hepatological disorder despite being driven substantially by endocrine and metabolic dysfunction. This review proposes a unified endocrine framework organised around seven hormonal axes, presenting each in terms of molecular pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and therapeutic implications. Insulin resistance is the central driver, coupling chronic caloric excess to hepatic de novo lipogenesis through selective hepatic insulin resistance, although genetic variants in PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 can uncouple steatosis from metabolic risk. Adipose tissue dysfunction contributes through adipocyte senescence, adipokine imbalance, and inflammatory adipose-liver signalling. Reduced hepatic thyroid hormone sensitivity, even in euthyroid individuals, predicts steatosis and fibrosis and underpins the first approved liver-directed therapy. Gonadal steroids exert sexually dimorphic effects, with testosterone deficiency, menopausal oestrogen loss, and polycystic ovary syndrome representing distinct risk states. Glucocorticoid dysregulation is stage-dependent, shifting from enhanced hepatic cortisol clearance in steatosis to local amplification in steatohepatitis. The gut-liver-endocrine axis, encompassing incretin, bile acid, and fibroblast growth factor signalling, has proved the most therapeutically tractable. Reduced GH/IGF-1 signalling, whether from pituitary disease or obesity-induced functional suppression, promotes both steatosis and fibrogenesis. Biological sex and life-course influences spanning developmental programming and ageing further modify these determinants. Two agents, resmetirom and semaglutide, now have US FDA accelerated approval for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis, supporting the principle that correcting axis-specific endocrine dysfunction can produce measurable hepatic benefit; however, both approvals are accelerated and await confirmatory outcome data, while others remain investigational. An endocrine framework offers both a coherent account of pathogenesis and a rational basis for biomarker-guided, phenotype-targeted therapy.

papers.title: Multi-omics Profiling Reveals the Effects of Xihuangcao on Hepatic Fibrosis Attenuation through Gut Microbiota and Metabolic Reprogramming.
papers.abstract: In various chronic liver diseases, hepatic fibrosis represents a frequent pathological event. This process involves the activation of hepatic stellate cells, along with the consequent excessive deposition of extracellular matrix. Emerging evidence highlights the contribution of gut microbiota dysbiosis and intestinal barrier dysfunction to its progression, underscoring the potential of targeting the liver-gut axis. Xihuangcao, a traditional Chinese medicinal herb used for acute cholecystitis and jaundice hepatitis, exhibits antifibrotic activity, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, hepatic fibrosis models were established to evaluate the antifibrotic effects of 3 botanical sources of Xihuangcao ( Isodon lophanthoides (Buch.-Ham. ex D.Don) H.Hara, Isodon lophanthoides var. graciliflorus (Benth.) H.Hara, and Isodon serra Kudô) through integrating histopathological, transcriptomics, metabolomics, 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) sequencing, and network pharmacology analyses. The results indicated that all 3 botanical sources of Xihuangcao markedly alleviated hepatic fibrosis and reduced collagen deposition. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that Xihuangcao down-regulated profibrotic mediators (Toll-like receptor 5, transforming growth factor-β, and platelet-derived growth factor) and modulated mitogen-activated protein kinase, steroid biosynthesis, bile secretion, and retinol metabolism pathways, highlighting its coordinated suppression of inflammation-driven fibrogenic activation in hepatic fibrosis. Liver metabolomics revealed Xihuangcao's effect on restoration of energy metabolism, amino acid turnover, and redox homeostasis. Xihuangcao also corrected fibrosis-induced gut dysbiosis, characterized by reduced Verrucomicrobia and increased S24-7 abundance, while suppressing pathogenic genera such as Clostridium and Prevotella . Moreover, Xihuangcao decreased profibrotic metabolites (androstan-3α,17β-diol) and suppressed choline-related metabolic pathways associated with fibrogenic signaling. Network pharmacology and experimental validation further identified PI3K/Akt inhibition as a key mechanism suppressing hepatic stellate cell activation.
