In summary, this study, based on integrative multi-omics analyses (metabolomics, transcriptomics, and 16S rRNA sequencing), found that Xihuangcao alleviates liver fibrosis by modulating inflammatory responses, metabolic disorders, and gut microbiota dysbiosis via the gut-liver axis. Furthermore, network pharmacology combined with in vitro experiments revealed that inhibition of hepatic stellate cell activation through the PI3K/Akt pathway may be the critical mechanism underlying its therapeutic efficacy.

papers.title: A multi-omics characterization of the gut microbiota of weaned piglets in response to Lactobacillus plantarum supplementation.
papers.abstract: Weaning is a critical developmental stage in piglets and is frequently associated with intestinal dysfunction, diarrhea, and growth retardation due to abrupt dietary and environmental changes. Probiotics have been explored as antibiotic alternatives to alleviate postweaning stress, and Lactobacillus plantarum has shown potential for modulating the gut microbiota and improving intestinal health. However, most previous studies have relied on single-omics approaches, limiting mechanistic understanding of host-microbiome interactions. This study employed an integrated multi-omics approach combining ileal transcriptomics, fecal microbiomics, and metabolomics to investigate the effects of dietary L. plantarum supplementation in weaned piglets. Six piglets were assigned to either a control or L. plantarum -supplemented group for two weeks. RNA sequencing, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and gas chromatography mass spectrometry based metabolomics were conducted, followed by integrative analysis using MIMOSA2 and MetaboAnalyst. Transcriptomic analysis identified 1,229 differentially expressed genes enriched in immune-related pathways, including NF-κB and IgA signaling, as well as epithelial barrier regulation. Microbiome profiling revealed increased microbial diversity, enrichment of Lactobacillus , and reduced abundance of Shigella . Functional prediction suggested enhanced innate immune responsiveness. Integrated metabolome-transcriptome analysis highlighted lipid and amino acid metabolic pathways linking microbial metabolites with host gene expression. Overall, L. plantarum supplementation induced coordinated host-microbiome adaptations associated with reduced oxidative stress, improved intestinal barrier stability, and enhanced immune resilience. These findings provide mechanistic evidence supporting L. plantarum as a promising nutritional strategy to mitigate postweaning stress and improve piglet intestinal health.

papers.title: Nutritional strategies using synbiotics and organic acids to enhance piglet post-weaning growth and gut health.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of dietary supplementation with probiotics (PRO), synbiotics (SYN), and SYN + benzoic acid (SYP) on growth performance, stress response, nutrient digestibility, blood parameters, immune status, and intestinal health of weanling pigs. Four hundred weaned pigs (Landrace × Yorkshire × Duroc) were allocated to four treatment groups: control (basal diet), PRO ( Bacillus licheniformis ), SYN ( Bacillus licheniformis + dietary fiber), and SYP. The feeding trial lasted for 28 days. Notably, pigs in the SYN and SYP groups showed greater average daily gain during phase 1 ( p = 0.038), phase 2 ( p = 0.008), and the overall period ( p = 0.011) compared with those in the control group. Gain-to-feed ratio was also improved during phase 2 ( p = 0.003) and the overall experimental period ( p = 0.012). The SYP group demonstrated significantly improved dry matter digestibility during phase 2 ( p < 0.05). Serum IL-1β concentrations tended to decrease in pigs fed SYN and SYP diets. In addition, SYN and SYP supplementation increased the concentration of the tight junction protein zona occludens-1 (ZO-1) in the jejunum ( p = 0.022). Histological analysis showed greater villus height in the duodenum ( p = 0.013) and jejunum ( p = 0.038) of pigs fed SYN and SYP diets. Overall, dietary supplementation with synbiotics, particularly in combination with benzoic acid, improved growth performance and intestinal health in weanling pigs.

papers.title: Dietary supplementation with coated zinc oxide enhanced growth performance by modulating systemic immunity and microbial composition in weaned pigs.
papers.abstract: Dietary zinc oxide (ZnO) is widely adopted in the swine industry to alleviate post-weaning diarrhea and promote the growth performance of weaned pigs. However, its low rate of absorption in the gastrointestinal tract leads to excessive excretion, which causes severe environmental pollution. To overcome this limitation, dietary coated ZnO (CZO) has been studied to enhance zinc absorption and mitigate its environmental influence. In the present study, we investigated the effects of dietary CZO on growth performance, frequency of diarrhea, nutrient digestibility, hematological and immune responses, and fecal microbiota of weaned pigs. A total of 72 weaned pigs (7.30 ± 0.01 kg of average initial body weight; 28 days old) were randomly assigned to three dietary treatments (4 pigs/pen; 6 replicates/treatment): basal weaner diet (CON), CON with 2,500 ppm of ZnO (HZO), and CON with 200 mg/kg of CZO. The experiment was conducted for 6 weeks. The CZO group increased ( p < 0.05) average daily gain and gain to feed ratio and showed tendency to reduce ( p = 0.094) the frequency of diarrhea compared with the CON group during the first two weeks after weaning. The CZO group showed a tendency for the lowest levels of serum tumor necrosis factor-α ( p = 0.072) on day 7 and hematocrit ( p = 0.083) on day 14 and the highest ( p = 0.072) levels of the immunoglobulin M on day 14 among the treatment groups. The HZO group tended to have the lowest ( p = 0.078) serum cortisol levels on day 7 among all treatments. At the genus level of gut microbiota analysis, the dietary CZO group showed a higher ( p < 0.05) relative abundance of Prevotella, Eubacterium , and Lactobacillus than pigs treated with the CON diet. The HZO group showed a higher ( p < 0.05) relative abundance of Eubacterium and Lactobacillus than the CON group. Our results demonstrated that dietary CZO supplementation enhanced growth performance and reduced the incidence of diarrhea by modulating systemic immune responses and shifting fecal microbial compositions in weaned pigs, suggesting its potential as an alternative to the high dose ZnO diets.

papers.title: Effects of fructooligosaccharides and inulin on growth performance, immunity and the gut microbiome in weaned piglets.
papers.abstract: Prebiotics such as fructooligosaccharides and inulin are biological activators that selectively stimulate the growth and activity of beneficial bacteria in the gastrointestinal tract. However, their specific effects when applied during the weaning period in piglets remains limited. Therefore, this study evaluated the effects of fructooligosaccharides and inulin supplementation in weaned piglets on growth performance, nutrient digestibility, immune response, and gut microbiota composition with the aim of exploring their potential benefits for piglet health during the weaning transition. A total of 72 weaned piglets (28 days of age) were allocated to three dietary groups: CON (basal diet), FOS (CON + 0.3% fructooligosaccharides), and INU (CON + 3% inulin) to investigate the effects of fructan supplementation. Growth performance, nutrient digestibility, blood profiles, immune responses, and fecal microbiota were evaluated. Although fructan supplementation did not induce significant changes in growth performance or nutrient digestibility, it significantly increased serum immunoglobulin A levels. Furthermore, the fecal microbiota of the fructan supplemented piglets was enriched with short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, including Phascolarctobacterium , Agathobacter , Clostridium sensu stricto , and Flavonifractor . Fructan supplementation in the diets of weaned piglets positively influenced immune response and gut microbiota composition, suggesting its potential to enhance gut health during the weaning period.

papers.title: Gut microbiome-shaped chemotherapy responses across cancer types: mechanisms of resistance, biomarkers, and targeted interventions.
papers.abstract: Cytotoxic chemotherapy remains an important component of multimodal treatment for many solid tumors, but resistance and dose-limiting toxicities continue to constrain clinical benefit. The gut microbiome can influence chemotherapy response through microbial drug biotransformation, metabolite signaling, intestinal-barrier integrity, systemic immune regulation, and tumor-cell stress and death pathways. Across solid tumors, the evidence is strongest in colorectal cancer, where clinical associations are supported by increasingly detailed mechanistic and interventional studies; evidence in many extraintestinal cancers remains less mature and is dominated by smaller observational cohorts and selected preclinical models. Importantly, gut-derived systemic effects should be distinguished from local or tumor-associated microbial mechanisms, and direct tumor-cell resistance should be separated from altered drug exposure and toxicity-mediated reductions in relative dose intensity. Microbiota-associated and metabolic biomarkers and microbiota-targeted interventions show potential for treatment stratification, toxicity prediction, and therapeutic modulation, but clinical translation remains limited by heterogeneous cohorts, incomplete causal validation, variable engraftment and strain specificity, and safety and standardization requirements. Overall, the microbiome is best viewed as a cancer- and regimen-specific modifier of chemotherapy rather than a universal determinant of response. Prospective, mechanism-matched studies are needed to establish whether microbiome-guided strategies can improve treatment efficacy, tolerance, and completion.

papers.title: Lipid metabolism: a potential checkpoint for cGAS-STING regulation in colorectal cancer.
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy for colorectal cancer (CRC) continues to face significant challenges, particularly in patients with microsatellite stable (MSS) tumors. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway is a key regulator of innate immunity and has emerged as a promising target for enhancing anti-tumor immune responses. Meanwhile, lipid metabolic reprogramming is a defining hallmark of CRC and contributes to tumor progression, evasion, and therapeutic resistance. Although direct evidence linking lipid metabolism to cGAS-STING signaling in CRC remains limited, accumulating studies from diverse disease models suggest extensive interactions between these two processes. This review summarizes the major features of lipid metabolic reprogramming in CRC and discusses current understanding of cGAS-STING signaling in tumor immunity. We further examine potential mechanisms by which lipid metabolism may influence cGAS-STING activity, including the regulation of mitochondrial DNA release, intracellular trafficking of signaling components and lipid-associated post-translational modifications. Emerging evidence also indicates that cGAS-STING signaling can affect lipid metabolic pathways by regulating lipid metabolic homeostasis and inducing lipid peroxidation-driven ferroptosis. Importantly, microbiota-derived lipid metabolites exert context-dependent effects on cGAS-STING signaling to balance intestinal inflammation and anti-tumor immunity. Finally, we discuss therapeutic strategies targeting lipid metabolism and cGAS-STING signaling, with a particular focus on approaches that may enhance anti-tumor immunity through coordinated metabolic-immune modulation. By bridging metabolic reprogramming with innate immune sensing, we propose that modulating the lipid-cGAS-STING axis could break immune tolerance and offer a distinct therapeutic window for CRC.

papers.title: Gut microbiota disturbance disrupts osteonal organization and mechanical competence during postnatal cortical bone maturation in rabbits with local metabolic and transcriptional remodeling.
papers.abstract: Bone strength depends not only on bone mass and mineral density but also on cortical tissue organization and material quality. Osteons are key structural units of cortical bone, yet whether gut microbiota disturbance affects cortical bone maturation at the osteon level remains unclear. We first characterized cortical canal remodeling and osteonal organization in New Zealand rabbits at 1, 2, and 3 months of age. Antibiotic-induced microbiota disturbance (AIMD) was then applied during this early osteon-forming window, followed by assessments of gut microbiota composition, osteon morphology, cortical bone micro-CT parameters, mechanical performance, femoral metabolomics, and cortical bone transcriptomics. AIMD reduced gut microbial diversity and altered microbial community structure. At 3 months of age, AIMD-treated rabbits showed impaired osteonal organization, including a reduced proportion of secondary osteons and altered osteon morphology. These osteon-level changes were accompanied by decreased maximum load and stiffness, whereas conventional micro-CT parameters of cortical geometry and mineral density remained unchanged. Multi-omics analyses further revealed local metabolic and transcriptional remodeling involving lipid-related metabolites, bone matrix regulation, osteocyte communication, and metabolic enzyme programs. These findings suggest that early gut microbiota disturbance impairs osteon-level cortical bone maturation and reduces mechanical competence. Osteonal organization may therefore represent a sensitive layer of cortical bone quality affected by gut microbiota disturbance during postnatal skeletal development.

papers.title: Oliceridine and morphine differentially modulate the gut microbiota-intestinal barrier axis in a rat postoperative pain model.
papers.abstract: Oliceridine is a novel G protein-biased μ-opioid receptor agonist with potentially improved gastrointestinal tolerability compared with conventional opioids. However, its impact on postoperative intestinal homeostasis-specifically the gut microbiota and intestinal barrier-remains poorly understood. A postoperative pain model was established in male Sprague-Dawley rats using the Brennan plantar incision method. Animals were randomly assigned to four groups: non-incision control (CON), plantar incision plus normal saline, plantar incision plus oliceridine (OLI, 1 mg/kg subcutaneous bolus followed by continuous infusion at 1 mg/kg/day for 72 h), and plantar incision plus morphine (MF, 5 mg/kg subcutaneous bolus followed by continuous infusion at 5 mg/kg/day for 72 h). Analgesic efficacy was assessed by mechanical withdrawal threshold (MWT) and area under the curve (AUC). Intestinal morphology, epithelial Claudin-1 expression by immunofluorescence (n = 4 per group), gut microbiota composition (16S rRNA gene sequencing, n = 6 per group), and host ileal transcriptomic profiles (RNA-seq, n = 3 per group) were evaluated. Oliceridine and morphine produced comparable analgesia, as reflected by MWT AUC (P < 0.0001 vs. NS; OLI vs. MF: P = 0.8770). Both opioids alleviated postoperative mechanical hypersensitivity. Compared with NS, opioid treatment increased the relative abundance of Limosilactobacillus and Lactobacillus and decreased Streptococcus . Exploratory microbiome analysis identified a potential Lactobacillus -related signal, but no genus-level difference between the OLI and MF groups remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Transcriptomic analysis revealed distinct ileal gene-expression profiles between the OLI and MF groups. Relative to MF, OLI was associated with higher expression of genes related to epithelial barrier integrity and brush border function and lower expression of genes involved in immune-related pathways. Histologically, both opioids attenuated intestinal injury compared with NS, with no significant difference between OLI and MF. In contrast, relative Claudin-1 fluorescence intensity was significantly higher in the OLI group than in the MF group (P = 0.036), providing protein-level support for the barrier-related transcriptomic findings. Integrated correlation analysis identified associations between Lactobacillus -related taxa and host genes linked to barrier function and metabolism (|r| > 0.6, P < 0.01). Oliceridine and morphine produced comparable analgesia. Exploratory microbiome analysis identified a potential Lactobacillus -related signal, but no genus-level differences remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Oliceridine was associated with a distinct ileal transcriptomic profile and higher Claudin-1 fluorescence intensity than morphine, although histological injury did not differ between the two groups. The functional significance of these molecular differences requires further investigation.

papers.title: Silybum marianum peptide-rich fraction alleviates acute liver injury by inhibiting TRAF3/NIK/NF-κB and is associated with changes in gut microbiota composition.
papers.abstract: Acute liver injury (ALI) is a severe and prevalent condition that can progress to irreversible liver damage and failure. This study aimed to investigate the prophylactic hepatoprotective potential of Silybum marianum peptides (SMP) in ALI and elucidate its underlying mechanisms. Using a carbon tetrachloride (CCl 4 )-induced ALI mouse model, we evaluated the dose-dependent effects of SMP. Additionally, we explored the modulatory effects of SMP on the NF-κB pathway, gut microbiota composition, and metabolite profiles. The role of SMP in the TRAF3/NIK/NF-κB signaling axis was further validated in a NIK-overexpressing Hepa1-6 cell model. Our results demonstrated that 14-day SMP administration did not significantly affect body weight, fasting blood glucose levels, or liver and spleen weights, and no significant difference in serum ALT activity was observed. Notably, SMP (200 mg/kg) significantly alleviated CCl 4 -induced liver injury, as evidenced by enhanced hepatic antioxidant capacity, reduced expression of proinflammatory cytokines, and attenuated immune cell infiltration. Furthermore, SMP was associated with changes in gut microbiota composition and community structure in CCl 4 -induced ALI mice. Mechanistically, SMP suppressed the TRAF3/NIK/NF-κB pathway. These findings highlight SMP as a promising candidate for the prevention of CCl 4 -induced ALI, acting through multimodal mechanisms involving anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and gut microbiota-associated pathways.

papers.title: GART expression is associated with a proliferative and purine-metabolic ISC-like epithelial state in ulcerative colitis.
papers.abstract: To characterize the epithelial state associated with GART expression in ulcerative colitis (UC) and determine whether this association reflects a GART-specific program or a broader proliferative and purine-metabolic phenotype. Four independent bulk transcriptomic cohorts were analyzed and synthesized by random-effects meta-analysis. Human colonic scRNA-seq datasets (GSE214695 and SCP259) were integrated, with principal comparisons repeated using donor-aware pseudobulk or mixed-effects approaches and adjustment for sequencing depth, gene detection, and cell-cycle covariates. GART detection was defined from raw counts and tested using alternative thresholds. Pseudotime, scTenifoldKnk, CellChat/LIANA, and transcriptional-network analyses were used as exploratory analyses. Spatial transcriptomics (GSE189184), human colonic multiplex immunofluorescence, and acute DSS-induced colitis tissues were used for tissue-level localization. Across the four bulk cohorts, GART expression showed an overall increase in UC (pooled Hedges' g = 0.743, 95% CI 0.239-1.248; P = 0.0183). In the single-cell atlas, GART detection localized preferentially to an ISC-like epithelial compartment, although the magnitude of the UC-associated detection difference varied between cohorts. Within UC ISC-like cells, donor-paired pseudobulk analyses identified proliferative and nucleotide-metabolic transcriptional differences associated with GART detection. Across the broader ISC-like epithelial atlas, donor-aware module analyses showed positive associations of GART detection with purine-biosynthesis, DNA-replication, DNA-repair, and mitotic programs, and these associations remained positive within cell-cycle strata. Comparison with other de novo purine-synthesis enzymes did not support a uniquely GART-specific alteration. Exploratory network analyses linked the GART-associated state to proliferative and nucleotide-metabolic programs but did not establish functional dependence. In seven independent spatial donors, the single-cell-derived epithelial program was consistently higher in GART-detected than GART-undetected epithelial regions (mean within-donor difference = 0.0262, 95% CI 0.0140-0.0407; exact P = 0.0156). Human tissue immunofluorescence further showed co-enrichment of GART with OLFM4-positive ISC-like, MYBL2/Ki67-positive proliferative, and MIF/CD74-associated inflammatory regions across the corresponding panel-specific participant sets. GART identifies a proliferative and purine-metabolic ISC-like epithelial state in UC but is not established as a specific driver of epithelial regeneration. The findings support an association between GART detection, nucleotide-demand programs, proliferative epithelial activity, and the inflammatory tissue context, providing a framework for future direct functional studies.

papers.title: Gut microbiota and serum metabolomics in children with human parainfluenza virus infection.
papers.abstract: Based on gut microbiota and serum untargeted metabolomics analyses, this study investigated changes in gut microbiota structure and serum metabolic profiles in children infected with human parainfluenza virus (HPIV). By integrating multi-omics data, we aimed to explore interactions between gut dysbiosis and serum metabolic disorders, and their potential roles in HPIV pathogenesis, to provide preliminary evidence for microbiota--targeted and metabolic intervention strategies. Clinical data and laboratory results were collected from 230 hospitalized children (<14 years) with HPIV infection. Subsequently, 31 HPIV-infected children and 12 healthy controls were enrolled. Fecal samples were analyzed via 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum samples via liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)-based untargeted metabolomics, followed by integrated multi-omics analysis. Children with severe HPIV infection had longer hospital stays and higher frequencies of wheezing, tachypnea, dyspnea, and vomiting. HPIV infection was associated with gut dysbiosis: opportunistic pathogens ( Anaerococcus , Peptoniphilus , Finegoldia ) were enriched, while beneficial commensals ( Blautia , Bifidobacterium , Faecalibacterium ) were reduced. Metabolomics identified 579 upregulated and 211 downregulated metabolites, primarily enriched in alpha-linolenic acid, butanoate, glycerophospholipid, starch/sucrose, and glycine/serine/threonine metabolism pathways. Correlation analysis showed that enriched opportunistic pathogens positively correlated with pro-inflammatory lipids (e.g., acetoacetic acid, 3-hydroxybutyric acid) and negatively with protective metabolites (e.g., alpha-linolenic acid, sucrose, L-threonine), while Blautia showed opposite patterns. The four key genera and five metabolites demonstrated exploratory discriminatory capacity for HPIV infection (AUC: 0.81 and 0.98, respectively), serving as candidate biomarkers for further validation. HPIV infection may be associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis and serum metabolic disturbances in children, potentially via the gut-lung axis, and these alterations may be involved in modulating pulmonary antiviral immune and inflammatory responses. This multi-omics study provides preliminary evidence for future research on prevention and treatment strategies targeting the gut microbiota or metabolic pathways in children with HPIV infection.

papers.title: Comment on "Mechanisms of gut microbiota metabolite-mediated gut-heart Axis in heart failure: An integrative study based on network pharmacology".
Moxibustion and the gut microbiota-inflammation axis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical and preclinical studies.
papers.abstract: Gut dysbiosis and aberrant inflammatory signaling are increasingly implicated in the pathogenesis of intestinal and extra-intestinal disorders. Moxibustion has been reported to modulate gut microbiota composition and inflammatory responses, but its overall effects remain incompletely characterized. Objective: To evaluate the effects of moxibustion on gut microbiota-related outcomes and inflammatory mediators in clinical and preclinical studies. PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, CNKI, WanFang Data, and VIP were searched from database inception to December 31, 2024. Clinical and preclinical studies investigating moxibustion and reporting at least one gut microbiota-related outcome were included. Clinical and preclinical evidence was synthesized separately, with quantitative meta-analysis restricted to eligible preclinical animal outcomes. Microbiota outcomes were pooled using ratios of means (ROMs), whereas inflammatory mediators were synthesized using standardized mean differences (SMDs) under random-effects models. Metabolite- and pathway-related findings were narratively synthesized. Thirty-one reports representing 30 unique studies were included, comprising 25 preclinical animal studies (26 reports) and 5 clinical studies. In animal studies, moxibustion increased Chao1 (ROM = 1.079, 95% CI [1.034-1.127]; P = 0.0005), ACE (ROM = 1.100, 95% CI [1.044-1.160]; P = 0.0004), and Shannon diversity (ROM = 1.047, 95% CI [1.015-1.080]; P = 0.0037), whereas Simpson diversity was not significantly altered. No significant pooled effects were detected for the major phyla. Ruminococcus decreased (ROM = 0.643, 95% CI [0.426-0.972]; P = 0.0364), whereas the other taxa retained in the main analysis showed no statistically significant pooled effects. Moxibustion reduced TNF-α (SMD = -1.648, 95% CI [-2.659 to -0.637]; P = 0.0014) and IL-1β (SMD = -1.861, 95% CI [-2.419 to -1.303]; P < 0.0001), whereas IL-6 and IL-10 were not significantly altered. Clinical findings were sparse and directionally inconsistent. Certainty of evidence for the evaluable prespecified primary microbiota outcomes was very low. Three studies further suggested potential modulation of short-chain fatty acids, amino acid metabolism, and microbial functional pathways. Preclinical evidence indicates that moxibustion is associated with increased microbial richness and diversity and reduced selected pro-inflammatory mediators, while taxon-specific responses are highly heterogeneous and clinical confirmation remains insufficient. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD42025639714.

papers.title: Histidine alleviates copper-induced intestinal inflammation through oxidative stress-mediated mitochondrial damage and the Hif1α-Tnfα/Il1β pathway.
papers.abstract: Copper (Cu) is an essential trace element for vertebrates, but excessive intake can induce intestinal toxicity. Whether nutritional intervention can alleviate Cu overload-induced intestinal damage and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we combined in vivo animal experiments with in vitro cell models to investigate the protective effect of histidine against Cu-induced intestinal inflammation and its molecular mechanisms. Rainbow trout (weight: 7.24 ± 0.03 g) were fed diets containing 3.11 mg Cu/kg and 6.89 g His/kg (Control), 12.69 mg Cu/kg and 6.71 g His/kg (Cu), 3.24 mg Cu/kg and 10.94 g His/kg (His), 12.37 mg Cu/kg and 10.87 g His/kg (Cu+His) for 8 weeks. Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) were isolated from rainbow trout and incubated for 24-h in Cu (10 μM) and His (2.5 mM) solution. Histopathology, ultrastructural structure, oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, and inflammation were determined in the intestine and IECs; fluorescence staining (DCFH-DA and JC-1), immunoblotting, immunofluorescence, siRNA, and ChIP were performed on IECs. Our research results indicate that Cu can induce intestinal oxidative stress, which in turn leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and activation of the Hif1α-Tnfα/Il1β signaling axis, ultimately exacerbating intestinal inflammatory responses. In contrast, co-treatment with Cu and histidine markedly attenuated the intestinal inflammatory phenotype. Mechanistically, histidine exerts anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting oxidative stress, improving mitochondrial function and suppressing Hif1α, thereby preventing the occurrence of intestinal inflammation. This study is the first to elucidate the mechanism by which histidine alleviates Cu-induced intestinal inflammation and delineated the critical regulatory role of mitochondrial damage and the Hif1α-Tnfα/Il1β pathway in this process within a fish model. It provides a new theoretical basis for mitigating heavy metal toxicity through nutritional intervention.

papers.title: Beneficial Effects of Nuts on Cardiovascular and Metabolic Health: An Insight into the Gut-Cardiometabolic Axis.
papers.abstract: Cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) are major contributors to global morbidity and mortality. Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiota plays a central role in the pathogenesis and progression of CMDs by regulating cardiometabolic endpoints, including lipid profiles, glucose homeostasis, immunity, inflammation, and oxidative stress. Nuts are nutrient-dense foods rich in unsaturated fatty acids, dietary fiber, polyphenols, vitamins, and minerals that interact with the gut microbiota. Additionally, nut intake has been associated with improved cardiometabolic health outcomes. This review examines current evidence on the effects of tree nut consumption on the gut-cardiometabolic axis, with an emphasis on clinical and mechanistic studies across different types of tree nuts. Clinical evidence of the capacity of nut consumption to affect CMDs is summarized. The bidirectional interaction between nut-derived microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, urolithins, phenolic acids, valerolactones, and gut microbiota, is highlighted. In addition, mechanisms by which changes in the nut-associated gut microbiome affect the CMDs via regulating lipids, glucose, energy homeostasis, and immunity modulation are discussed. The available evidence, although mostly associative, supports the potential favorable effects of nuts in modulating gut microbial composition and function in ways that may improve cardiometabolic health. However, future studies are needed to address limitations in current studies, including substantial heterogeneity across studies, the lack of established causal mechanisms, long-term clinical outcomes, and to investigate personalized responses to nut consumption given interindividual variability in gut microbiota.

papers.title: Methods and Techniques for Closed-Loop Gastrointestinal Pacing.
papers.abstract: Gastrointestinal slow waves are rhythmic electrical events that contribute to the coordination of motility. Functional motility disorders such as gastroparesis are linked to abnormal slow wave activity, and current treatments do not target the underlying electrical dysfunction. Gastrointestinal electrical pacing restores normal rhythms, but open-loop pacing lacks adaptation to underlying slow wave activity, leading to reduced energy efficiency and potential overstimulation. A novel closed-loop pacing system was developed to detect gastric and intestinal slow waves and dynamically pace in response to the underlying rhythm. High-resolution electrode arrays were placed on the serosal surface of anesthetized pigs for simultaneous pacing and mapping. The control strategy comprised two steps: (i) continuous detection and classification of slow waves as normal rhythm (stomach: 15-25 s; small intestine: 3-5 s) or abnormal rhythm; and (ii) pacing delivery and entrainment assessment, with pulses (100-400 ms, 3-8 mA) triggered by abnormal rhythms or failed entrainment. Detection of slow wave events achieved an accuracy of 78% for both the stomach and the small intestine. Entrainment detection yielded an accuracy of 73% for the stomach and 67% for the small intestine. Closed-loop pacing successfully restored abnormal gastric and small intestinal slow wave periods to normal physiological ranges and reduced the number of pulses delivered by 60% compared to open-loop pacing. Closed-loop pacing significantly reduced pulse delivery, demonstrating the feasibility of a targeted, adaptive approach that may reduce pacing burden, although effects on motility and gastric emptying warrant further investigation.

papers.title: Targeting ubiquitin-dependent mitochondrial autophagy and apoptosis in sarcopenia: the therapeutic potential of phytochemicals.
papers.abstract: Sarcopenia is a progressive degenerative disease of skeletal muscle closely associated with aging, disuse, and chronic diseases, affecting approximately 10-16% of the global older adult population. Its core pathological basis lies in the disruption of skeletal muscle cell proteostasis and mitochondrial dysfunction. At the molecular level, excessive degradation of structural proteins mediated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system forms an intertwined vicious cycle with the inability of ubiquitin-dependent mitophagy to clear damaged organelles, ultimately triggering irreversible cell death programmes within an oxidative stress and inflammatory microenvironment. Due to the high complexity and molecular crosstalk within this cell fate-determining network, traditional single-target interventions often yield limited therapeutic efficacy. In recent years, phytochemicals (such as polyphenols, flavonoids, alkaloids, and coumarins) have demonstrated significant therapeutic potential in the field of sarcopenia due to their unique multi-target, multi-pathway synergistic regulatory advantages. This article reviews the dual-faceted regulatory mechanisms of ubiquitination in skeletal muscle mitochondrial quality control, protein hydrolysis, and apoptosis escape and provides an analysis of how phytochemicals achieve autophagy-promoting, anti-apoptotic, and anti-degradative skeletal muscle protection. However, oral bioavailability is often below 1%, microbiota-dependent metabolism, and the absence of phase III clinical trials have hindered the translational application of phytochemicals. This paper explores the use of nano-delivery systems to overcome the bioavailability bottleneck of phytochemicals, as well as translational application strategies based on the gut-muscle axis to reshape the in vivo metabolism of natural products. This review aims to provide a solid theoretical foundation for the development of novel phytochemical-derived drugs targeting ubiquitination and apoptosis networks and to chart a course for reversing skeletal muscle ageing and enhancing human healthspan.

papers.title: Disentangling microbiota-dependent and -independent impacts of antibiotics on host physiology.
papers.abstract: Antibiotics are believed to affect host physiology by altering the gut microbiota. However, it remains unclear which effects of antibiotics are microbiota dependent and which are microbiota independent. Here we present a resource encompassing host and microbiota responses to antibiotic treatment and a computational tool with which to analyse them. Metagenomic and transcriptomic analyses of conventional and germ-free mice revealed that antibiotic administration routes and their combinations affect host and microbiota responses. We developed CompoRes-a computational tool that distinguishes the microbiota-independent impact of antibiotic-induced perturbations, revealing that antibiotics directly impact host physiology. We found that diurnal expression of major histocompatibility complex class II in the mouse colon is controlled by glucose via feeding. This pattern was lost during antibiotic treatment as vancomycin altered feeding behaviour in a microbiota-independent and evolutionarily conserved manner. Together, our study establishes a direct, non-microbial pathway by which antibiotics reshape host immunity and circadian physiology.

papers.title: Enantiomer-specific effects of metconazole disrupt soil microbiota, gut homeostasis, and genomic responses of Eisenia fetida.
papers.abstract: The selective use of highly active, low-risk enantiomers in place of racemic fungicides represents a sustainable approach to balancing agricultural productivity with environmental safety. Little is known about the enantioselective toxicity and environmental disturbances of the chiral triazole fungicide metconazole (MEZ) on the soil ecosystem. This study revealed that rac-MEZ dissipated faster than cis-MEZs in soil, but rac-MEZ induced a greater decrease in bacterial diversity and network complexity. The longer persistence of cis-MEZs possibly led to greater bioaccumulation in earthworms (Eisenia fetida). Enantioselectivity was observed for two cis-MEZs; cis-1R,5S-MEZ exhibited more severe acute toxicity in earthworms than cis-1S,5R-MEZ. This may be attributed to the potential detoxifying protein (CYP4V), which binds weakly with cis-1R, 5S-MEZ. This weaker detoxification capacity potentially resulted in oxidative stress response system collapse in earthworms, leading to excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and disturbance of antioxidant and detoxification enzymes (such as CAT, SOD, and GST). The ROS dysregulation caused by cis-1R, 5S-MEZ induced severe ecotoxicity, including DNA damage, heme metabolism disruption, and downregulation of transcriptional ovo-spermathecal apparatus development and genomic diversification, possibly resulting in higher ipotoxicity, genotoxicity, and reproductive toxicity. Therefore, cis-1R,5S-MEZ is more toxic to earthworms and their ecological functions, suggesting a less favorable environmental risk profile for potential agricultural use.

papers.title: Unraveling gut-brain crosstalk: Lessons from Drosophila and other insect models.
papers.abstract: Bidirectional communication between the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system is emerging as a fundamental regulatory principle across animal phyla. Insects, the model organism Drosophila melanogaster in particular, have become powerful models for dissecting this crosstalk at cellular and molecular resolution. Recent advances reveal conserved enteroendocrine neuropeptide signaling pathways and neuronal circuits that regulate feeding behavior, metabolism, and physiological homeostasis. Here we review progress over the past decade, highlight mechanistic insights that are broadly relevant to mammalian biology, and discuss open questions that insect models are positioned to address.

papers.title: Rethinking Pathogenesis of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis.
papers.abstract: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease characterized by progressive fibroinflammatory injury of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts that may lead to cirrhosis, hepatobiliary malignancy, and death, with liver transplantation representing the only effective intervention in end-stage disease. Rather than a single dominant pathomechanism, the data support a model in which four axes - bile acid metabolism, the intestinal microbiome and gut barrier, biliary epithelial dysfunction, and Th17-skewed immune dysregulation - are reciprocally coupled and converge on a shared periductal fibrogenic output dominated by TGF-beta signaling. This review summarizes key mechanistic advances from genetic, epigenomic, single-cell, spatial transcriptomic, and microbiome studies. These investigations implicate antigen presentation pathways, Th17-skewed immune responses, cholangiocyte senescence and profibrotic signaling, and disrupted gut-liver communication as central drivers of chronic biliary injury. Emerging spatial and multi-omics approaches further reveal complex cellular crosstalk among cholangiocytes, immune cells, macrophages, and mesenchymal populations within portal inflammatory niches. We discuss evolving biomarkers and recent clinical trial data targeting bile acid metabolism, fibrosis, the microbiome, and immune pathways. In conclusion, research data suggests viewing PSC as a network disease, which provides a unifying framework for disease pathogenesis and may enable biomarker-guided patient stratification and mechanism-based therapy development targeting distinct pathogenic pathways.

papers.title: A microbiome-bile acid axis mediates protection from chronic liver disease in females.
papers.abstract: Sex-based differences in chronic liver disease (CLD) incidence and progression are well documented, yet the mechanistic basis of this sexual disparity remains elusive. Here, leveraging a large-scale metabolomics database comprising 9,254 individuals, we identify the endogenous bile acid, isoursodeoxycholic acid (isoUDCA), as a candidate mediator of female-associated hepatoprotection. We trace the origin of isoUDCA to a bacterial consortium, which is selectively enriched by estrogen through shaping a specialized intestinal microenvironment. Mechanistically, isoUDCA promotes the nuclear accumulation of SREBP2. This upregulates the intracellular transporter STARD4 and its functionally coupled downstream enzyme CYP7B1, thereby facilitating intracellular cholesterol handling and metabolic conversion. Collectively, our findings support a microbiome-bile acid-liver axis that may contribute to sex differences in CLD susceptibility and support further evaluation of isoUDCA as a potential therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: Combined exposure to polyethylene microplastics, copper, and Di(2-Ethylhexyl) phthalate reconfigures component-specific internal exposure profiles and triggers cross-level biological responses in earthworms.
papers.abstract: Microplastics, metals, and plastic additives commonly coexist in soils, but how their interactions reconfigure internal exposure and relate to biological responses across multiple levels We exposed Eisenia fetida to polyethylene microplastics (PE), copper (Cu), and di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) singly and in binary and ternary combinations, integrating internal exposure, organismal phenotypes, redox biomarkers, histopathology, gut microbiota, and untargeted metabolomics. Combined exposure reconfigured rather than uniformly increased internal exposure: under ternary exposure, whole-body Cu decreased from 17.96 to 10.34 mg kg⁻¹ , whereas DEHP increased from 2735.76 to 8523.19 μg kg⁻¹ , while gut-retained PE varied among mixtures. Ternary exposure produced the strongest organismal effects, with mortality reaching 34%, body-weight loss 18.16%, reproductive and locomotor impairment, and ROS increasing 4.9-fold over the control. Gut bacterial responses were contaminant-specific: PE increased Chao1 richness from 1808 to 2579, while community composition differed among treatments (PERMANOVA, R² = 0.482, P = 0.001) and assembly shifted markedly under PE + DEHP and DEHP + Cu. Predicted microbial functions differed among treatments (R² = 0.525), with internal PE and Cu burdens significantly associated with KO profiles. Metabolomics identified 100, 66, and 124 candidate metabolites under PE, Cu, and DEHP, respectively, while Cu showed the clearest FDR-supported pathway enrichment. These findings reveal component-specific internal exposure linked to host, microbial, and metabolic responses.

papers.title: 2'-Fucosyllactose enhances indole-3-lactic acid production by Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 and alleviates colitis-associated bone loss: Associations with microbiota remodeling and intestinal AHR-related responses.
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease is frequently associated with an imbalance in bone remodeling and a decline in bone mass, however, there is a lack of systematic research on microbiome-based intervention strategies targeting colitis-associated bone loss. In this study, Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 (DNG-08) was selected from four candidate strains based on its favorable 2'-fucosyllactose (2'-FL) utilization and indole-3-lactic acid (ILA) production. Genomic annotation revealed that DNG-08 harbors functional genes related to fucosylated oligosaccharide utilization and the conversion of tryptophan to ILA. In a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model, combined intervention with DNG-08 and 2'-FL significantly alleviated colitis-associated phenotypes, and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels by 13.33%-58.69%, while increasing IL-10-1.23 times that of the DSS group. Simultaneously, the combined intervention improved trabecular bone microstructure, increasing the bone formation marker procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP) by 14.61%-56.37%, decreasing the bone resorption marker C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX-I) by 17.03%-21.77%, and upregulating the expression of Wnt3a, β-catenin, and Runx2. Gut microbiota analysis showed that combined intervention could partially reverse DSS-induced dysbiosis, enriching potentially beneficial bacterial taxa while reducing inflammation-associated genera. Notably, combined treatment group exhibited elevated serum ILA levels, increased colonic aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) fluorescence, and upregulatied CYP1A1 expression. Correlation analysis identified significant associations among serum ILA, AHR-related indicators, selected bacterial genera, and bone remodeling parameters. This study highlights that strain-substrate matching may serve as a precise synbiotic strategy to improve inflammation-related gut-bone axis dysfunction.

papers.title: The Potential Role of Gut Microbiota in Combating Mycobacterium tuberculosis Infection.
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( M.TB ) infection. Although there have been significant advances in the treatment of M.TB infection, it still faces significant challenges. The gut microbiota is a highly complex ecosystem that plays an important role in regulating metabolism, immune regulation, and maintaining healthy balance in the human body. More and more studies have found that while gut microbiota regulates the immune regulation process of pulmonary TB through the "gut-lung axis," infection with M.TB can also affect the microbial stability of gut microbiota, thereby affecting host health. This article summarized and discussed the changes of gut flora in TB patients, the possible relationship and impact between gut flora and M.TB infection, and summarized and looked forward to the potential of gut flora in the treatment of TB, in order to provide a reference for the prevention and treatment of gut microorganisms in anti- M.TB infection.

papers.title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
papers.abstract: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited. This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored. Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects. Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

papers.title: Osteopenia in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
papers.abstract: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a common type of scoliosis, which occurs in 10 to 18-year-old adolescents and is often accompanied by osteopenia, but the etiology of osteopenia is still unknown. Exploring the etiology may play an important role in fully understanding the pathogenesis of AIS and drawing new treatment ideas. Understanding the etiology of osteopenia in AIS. This article conducted a comprehensive search across PubMed, Web of Science (WOS), and CNKI for literature concerning osteopenia in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. The primary search strategy employed "(adolescent idiopathic scoliosis) AND (osteopenia)", supplemented by additional keywords encompassing "bone mineralization disorders", "hormones", "leptin", "calcitonin", "vitamin K", "treatment", etc. The review prioritized recent, high-quality literature. This review disclosed the research process of osteopenia in AIS and expounded its possible pathogenesis resulting in osteogenic and bone metabolic abnormalities. Meanwhile, this review summarized some other possible pathogenesis, like gut microbiota, nutritional factors resulting in osteopenia in AIS. Furtherly, the article revealed the relationship between osteopenia and AIS treatment outcome. Osteopenia in AIS patients is caused by multiple factors. During the treatment of AIS, it may be necessary to intervene in osteopenia.

papers.title: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Strains LP5 and BX62 Alleviate Liver Injury of NAFLD in Rats via Regulating Hepatic Cholesterol Metabolism and Antioxidant Signaling Pathways.
papers.abstract: Disorders of lipid metabolism and oxidative stress are pivotal factors in the advancement of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). This study aims to investigate the liver-protective effects of two Lactiplantibacillus plantarum (L. plantarum) strains, LP5 and BX62, either individually or in combined, on NAFLD in rats induced by high fat and cholesterol diet. Strain L. plantarum LP5 showed potential for modulating cholesterol metabolism, whereas L. plantarum BX62 exhibited enhanced antioxidant properties. All three intervention strategies alleviated liver injury, as evidenced by reduced hepatic lipid accumulation, intestinal permeability, inflammation, and liver injury markers. Notably, L. plantarum LP5 showed greater effects on reducing weight gain and hepatic steatosis, while L. plantarum BX62 provided additional protection against hepatic oxidative damage. Metabolic and molecular analyses suggested that the beneficial effects of L. plantarum LP5 were associated with altered bile acid homeostasis and increased expression of hepatic primary bile acid synthesis-related proteins (CYP7A1 and CYP8B1), whereas L. plantarum BX62 was associated with activation of the Nrf2-HO-1 antioxidant pathway (Nrf2, HO-1, and FTH). Furthermore, all intervention strategies activated AMPK signaling (p-AMPK/AMPK), accompanied by decreased expression of lipogenesis-related proteins (SREBP-1c, FASN, and SCD1) and increased expression of fatty acid oxidation-related proteins (PPARα and CPT1a), contributing to improved hepatic lipid metabolism. Collectively, our findings indicate that L. plantarum LP5 and L. plantarum BX62 alleviate HFHC diet-induced hepatic metabolic disturbances by complementary mechanisms involving cholesterol metabolism and antioxidant responses, highlighting their potential as dietary probiotics for supporting liver health and preventing NAFLD progression.

papers.title: Nutritional Innovations in Functional Foods: Exploring Postbiotics for Gut and Vascular Health Enhancement.
papers.abstract: The exploration of microbiome-targeted interventions in functional foods has accelerated, with postbiotics emerging as a compelling alternative to probiotics. Defined as non-viable microbial cells or their metabolic products, postbiotics demonstrate diverse bioactivities, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunomodulatory effects. These attributes enable modulation of the gut-vascular axis, a critical interface influencing systemic inflammation and cardiovascular risk. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), bioactive peptides, and microbial enzymes are among the most studied postbiotics with profound effects on gut integrity and vascular function. Mineral-enriched postbiotics, particularly those supplemented with zinc and selenium, offer further promise in managing metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disorders. This review critically evaluates the molecular mechanisms through which postbiotics modulate the gut-vascular axis. We discuss the pathways associated with the improvement or eradication of gut-vascular axis-related diseases, focusing on their impact on intestinal integrity, immune regulation, and vascular function. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of postbiotics as functional food ingredients and therapeutic agents for chronic disease management, particularly in metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disorders.

papers.title: Impact of mixed nut consumption on faecal lipid content and gut microbiota composition in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: Nuts are a source of dietary fibre and are considered a nutritious snack despite their high fat content. The effects of nut consumption on the microbiota and the role of nut-derived lipids in altering the large intestinal microbial community remain poorly understood. This study examined changes in faecal characteristics and microbiota composition in 15 healthy volunteers consuming unrestricted diets during a cross-over dietary intervention consisting of three weeks of daily mixed-nut consumption (30 g almonds, macadamias and pistachios) and three weeks of nut abstinence. Microscopic examination of faecal samples revealed lipid-containing nut particles following nut consumption, which were not observed during the nut abstinence. Mixed nut consumption was associated with a significant increase in total faecal lipid content compared with nut abstinence ( P < 0.05), suggesting incomplete digestion and absorption of nut-derived lipids. In contrast, faecal pH, dry matter, ash content, short-chain fatty acids and ammonium concentrations were not significantly altered by the intervention. 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis demonstrated substantial inter-individual variation in gut microbial community composition, with only modest differences associated with nut consumption. Predicted functional profiling suggested variation in pathways related to lipid metabolism between intervention periods. Overall, the findings indicate that a portion of consumed nut cells likely reaches the large intestine intact. Upon degradation of the nut cell wall, encapsulated lipids may become available to the colonic microbiota, potentially contributing to microbial metabolism and community responses observed.

papers.title: Gut microbiome-related plasma metabolites and risk of colorectal cancer.
papers.abstract: Perturbations in gut microbiome composition and altered levels of related metabolites may be related to colorectal cancer (CRC). This study assessed whether pre-diagnostic, circulating, microbiome-related metabolite concentrations were associated with CRC risk. We undertook a nested case-control study of 739 participants in the Colon Cancer Family Registry Cohort (312 cases, 427 controls). Median follow-up time from blood draw to diagnosis was 7 years. Pre-diagnostic plasma concentrations of 70 metabolites were quantified by targeted liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated for metabolite concentrations and CRC risk using multivariable conditional logistic regression models. Stratified analyses were conducted by sex, Lynch syndrome diagnosis, and age at tumor onset. The primary bile acids, cholate and chenodeoxycholate, were positively associated with CRC incidence, overall and among females. The odds of CRC were higher in individuals in the highest compared with the lowest quartiles of cholate (ORQ4vQ1=1.61, 95% CI=1.05-2.49) and chenodeoxycholate (ORQ4vQ1=1.60, 95% CI=1.03-2.50). Two short-chain fatty acids (caproate, valerate) and three metabolites involved in phenylalanine and tyrosine metabolism (cinnamoylglycine, phenylpropionate, 4-ethylphenylsulfate) were suggested to be associated, positively and negatively, respectively, with incident CRC but these associations did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. In stratified analyses, some differences were observed according to sex, Lynch syndrome diagnosis, and age at tumor onset. Circulating microbiome-related metabolites, including bile acids and short-chain fatty acids, may be associated with CRC risk. These findings provide insight into potential pathways linking the gut microbiome to colorectal carcinogenesis.

papers.title: Linking the fine structural characteristics of cereal β-glucans to their differential protective effects against colitis.
papers.abstract: Although cereal β-glucans exert protective effects against experimental colitis, the relationship between their fine structural and physicochemical properties and differential in vivo responses remains unclear. This study directly compared highland barley β-glucan (BBG) and oat β-glucan (OBG), two high-purity mixed-linkage β-(1 → 3)/(1 → 4)-D-glucans, under identical experimental conditions. BBG had a higher cellotriosyl-to-cellotetraosyl (DP3/DP4) ratio than OBG (2.33 vs. 1.51) and a lower weight-average molecular weight. In dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis mice, both β-glucans alleviated clinical signs of disease, while BBG showed greater protection at the tissue and biochemical levels. BBG preserved colon length at 4.88 cm, compared with 4.46 cm for OBG. It reduced myeloperoxidase activity, nitric oxide, and malondialdehyde levels to 1226 U g -1 , 0.42 μmol g -1 , and 78.8 nmol mg -1 , respectively, and fully restored Claudin-1 expression. BBG was also associated with enrichment of Ligilactobacillus , Limosilactobacillus , Romboutsia , and Turicibacter and suppression of Escherichia-Shigella . Fecal metabolomics showed higher levels of selected indole derivatives and taurine-conjugated bile acids, accompanied by lower uric acid and prostaglandin-related inflammatory metabolites. These in vivo differences were accompanied by distinct physicochemical behaviors. BBG showed faster self-aggregation, with a shorter lag time than OBG (112.9 vs . 256.0 min), accompanied by a markedly higher storage modulus (360 vs. 66 Pa). BBG also showed stronger intestinal-phase reassembly under simulated gastrointestinal conditions, approximately threefold greater bile acid retention during dynamic dialysis, and higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity (11.8% vs. 4.8%). Overall, the differential intestinal responses to BBG and OBG were accompanied by distinct physicochemical, microbial, and metabolic profiles, supporting a potential aggregation between cereal β-glucan fine structure, supramolecular behavior, and protective effects against colitis.

papers.title: Protein malnutrition facilitates intestinal colonization with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae through disrupted intestinal microbial metabolism.
papers.abstract: Pediatric infections with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (HR-Kp) disproportionately affect low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Malnutrition is an identified risk factor for infection with HR-Kp and other antimicrobial-resistant Enterobacterales, but the mechanistic underpinnings of this link and independence from other common exposures, like antibiotics, in children are unclear. Using a murine model of pediatric malnutrition, we found that mice fed a protein-deficient diet (PD) were more susceptible to colonization with HR-Kp at a 4-log lower challenge inoculum and developed a 3-log higher intestinal burden in comparison to adequately nourished mice. HR-Kp colonization in PD-fed mice persisted beyond 5 weeks, and colonization was transmitted to diet-matched cage mates. Antibiotic treatment resulted in similar HR-Kp colonization burdens regardless of diet, suggesting that nutrition-dependent colonization risk is driven by altered intestinal microbiota. Despite reduced dietary protein intake, intestinal amino acid content was maintained in PD-fed mice, supporting optimal HR-Kp growth. Furthermore, secondary bile acids, prototypic intestinal microbiota-derived molecules, were reduced in PD-fed mice, demonstrated an inverse correlation with HR-Kp burden in vivo , and partially inhibited the growth of HR-Kp in vitro . Collectively, these findings reveal a role for dietary protein intake in determining nutrition-dependent colonization resistance to HR-Kp.IMPORTANCEAntimicrobial-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae are responsible for a growing mortality burden worldwide, with disproportionate rates of infection in low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Several publications have demonstrated high rates of intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant K. pneumoniae in children admitted with severe malnutrition in sub-Saharan Africa. However, numerous confounding risk factors in malnourished children (antibiotic use, healthcare exposure, and immune dysfunction) make it difficult to assess the direct impact of nutrition on K. pneumoniae colonization. In this study, we utilized a novel mouse model of protein malnutrition to demonstrate that dietary protein deficiency renders mice susceptible to a higher burden of intestinal colonization at a lower inoculating dose of K. pneumoniae . Furthermore, reduced microbiota-derived bile acid metabolites correlate with increased burden of colonization in protein-deficient mice. These results are the first to establish a direct mechanistic link associating dietary protein deficiency, bile acid metabolism, and intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant K. pneumoniae .

papers.title: Myrica rubra juice attenuates DSS-induced colitis and is associated with changes in the gut microbiota-metabolite-host axis.
papers.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is characterized by chronic intestinal inflammation and impaired mucosal barrier function. Myrica rubra contains polyphenols and flavonoids, but the mechanisms underlying its potential protective effects in colitis remain unclear. We evaluated Myrica rubra juice (MRJ) in a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model of colitis and a TNF-α-injured colonic organoid model. The study combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted serum and fecal metabolomics, and molecular docking. MRJ treatment attenuated disease severity and was associated with increased expression of occludin and MUC2 in DSS-treated mice. MRJ also altered microbial diversity and taxonomic composition in a taxon-specific manner. Serum and fecal metabolomic profiles differed after MRJ treatment, including pathways related to amino acid and bile acid metabolism. Integrated analyses identified associations among microbial taxa, putatively annotated metabolites, and host inflammatory and barrier-related variables. Direct exposure to 20% (v/v) whole MRJ increased occludin immunofluorescence in TNF-α-injured colonic organoids cultured without a gut microbial community. This single-marker result is consistent with an epithelial response to whole MRJ under the applied in vitro conditions. Molecular docking generated predicted poses and docking scores for selected parent compound-protein pairs. These calculations did not demonstrate physical binding, functional inhibition, or target engagement in vivo . Together, the findings support a direct epithelial response and identify concurrent microbiota-associated changes. However, the present design could not determine whether these microbial changes contributed to protection. It also could not separate or quantify the host-directed and microbiota-mediated contributions or identify the active chemical species.

papers.title: Comparative dietary profiling of smoked and non-smoked paprika ( Capsicum annuum L.) in Wistar rats: metabolomic, biochemical and gut microbiota responses in a healthy animal model.
papers.abstract: Paprika ( Capsicum annuum L.) is a widely consumed spice whose bioactive composition is substantially influenced by processing conditions. Traditional smoking, as applied in the production of PDO Pimentón de la Vera, enriches paprika with wood smoke-derived phenolics while also introducing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), warranting an integrated evaluation of processing-related biological responses and safety considerations. This study compared physiological, biochemical, metabolomic, and cecal microbiota responses to dietary supplementation with smoked and non-smoked paprika in healthy Wistar rats. Thirty animals of both sexes (16 females and 14 males) received a control diet or diets supplemented with 5% smoked or non-smoked paprika for 30 days. Histological examination revealed no treatment-related alterations in the organs evaluated. Hematological and biochemical analyses showed diet- and sex-associated differences in hematocrit, plasma glucose, total antioxidant capacity, and lipid-related parameters, although all values remained within normal physiological ranges. Untargeted urinary metabolomics, restricted to males because of insufficient urine volume in females, identified features tentatively annotated as phenolic conjugates and other metabolites associated with paprika intake, with several signals showing higher abundance in the smoked paprika group. Cecal metagenomic analyses showed sex-dependent changes across taxon-level abundance, alpha diversity, and beta diversity. In females receiving smoked paprika, lower TC and LDL-C coincided with higher alpha diversity and lower cecal lipid content, suggesting a potential link between intestinal microbial ecology and lipid handling. Overall, paprika processing was associated with distinct biochemical, metabolomic, and cecal microbiota response patterns in this healthy animal model.

papers.title: Peptide profiling of casein peptide reveals its anti-diabetic effects via DPP-IV inhibition and IRS1/PI3K/AKT signaling.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a growing global health burden, increasing demand for safe food-derived strategies for glycemic control. Casein-derived peptides have potential metabolic benefits, but their antidiabetic mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, casein peptide (CNP), enriched in low-molecular-weight peptides (<3 kDa), was investigated as the principal bioactive intervention for T2DM regulation. LC-MS/MS identified 880 peptides; among the 50 most abundant, all were predicted to inhibit DPP-IV, 26 to inhibit α-glucosidase, and one to inhibit α-amylase. CNP inhibited DPP-IV in vitro in a concentration-dependent manner (IC 50 = 5.06 ± 0.41 mg mL -1 ) and crossed Caco-2 monolayers partly through endocytosis and PepT1-mediated transport. In HFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice, CNP improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, ameliorated dyslipidemia, attenuated tissue injury and systemic inflammation, and restored GLP-1/DPP-IV balance and IRS1/PI3K/AKT signaling. These findings identify CNP as a key food-derived bioactive peptide system that modulates T2DM through complementary effects on intestinal transport, incretin regulation, glucose-lipid homeostasis, inflammation, and insulin signaling, supporting its potential for development as a functional food ingredient for T2DM management.

papers.title: Gut microbial and metabolomic alterations associated with herpetic trigeminal neuralgia: an exploratory multi-omics study.
papers.abstract: Herpetic trigeminal neuralgia (HTN) is a neuropathic pain disorder caused by varicella-zoster virus invasion of the trigeminal nerve, but its mechanisms remain poorly elucidated. Accumulating evidence implicates gut microbiota dysbiosis and metabolic perturbations in modulating chronic pain via the gut-brain axis, yet their roles in HTN have not been systematically explored. Integrated multi-omics analysis was performed on 19 patients with HTN and 18 healthy controls. Fecal metagenomic sequencing characterized gut microbial composition and function. Untargeted metabolomics profiled metabolic signatures in fecal and circulating samples. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and random forest modeling screened pivotal microbial and metabolic features associated with HTN. Correlation analysis between differential metabolites and clinical pain scores validated the translational potential of identified alterations. HTN patients showed significantly reduced gut microbial diversity, with enriched Proteobacteria , depleted butyrate-producing bacteria (including Faecalibacterium , Roseburia , and Lachnospira ), and expanded opportunistic pathogens ( Escherichia coli and [ Ruminococcus ] gnavus ). Microbial pathways for pH homeostasis and oxidative stress defense were downregulated. Metabolomic analysis identified differential metabolites, primarily involving nicotinate/nicotinamide metabolism and retrograde endocannabinoid signaling. WGCNA and random forest analyses suggested fecal metabolites as potential candidate features, with associations between gut microbial dysregulation and systemic metabolic changes. Furthermore, screened metabolites correlated significantly with pain scores. This study provides multi-omics evidence of gut microbial and metabolic dysregulation in HTN, generating hypotheses for further mechanistic research. Large-scale, multicenter prospective cohorts with standardized metadata collection are needed to validate these findings.

papers.title: Heat-treated Lactiplantibacillus plantarum MYO Improves Muscle Strength and Modulates Gut Microbiota in Older Adults with Reduced Muscle Strength.
papers.abstract: Age-related sarcopenia is a condition characterized by a decline in muscle strength and physical function with aging, and its improvement is important given its close association with falls, fractures, and mortality. Recently, as the link between age-related gut microbiota dysbiosis and sarcopenia has been elucidated, modulation of the gut microbiota has gained attention as a therapeutic strategy for sarcopenia. In particular, with growing interest in paraprobiotics, various health-promoting effects-including gut microbiota modulation and improvement of muscle strength-have been reported. However, clinical evidence supporting the association between the gut microbiota and muscle strength remains limited. Accordingly, this clinical study was conducted to investigate the effects of heat-treated Lactiplantibacillus plantarum MYO (LPMYO) intake on quadriceps muscle strength, hand grip strength, muscle quality index (MQI) and gut microbiota composition in older adults with reduced muscle strength, and to examine the correlation between muscle strength and gut microbiota. After 12 weeks of heat-treated LPMYO supplementation, quadriceps muscle strength, hand grip strength and MQI were significantly improved compared with the placebo group. In addition, the abundance of beneficial bacteria, including Faecalibacterium , Lachnospira , Turicibacter , Megasphaera , and the [ Eubacterium ]_ ventriosum group, was significantly increased. Notably, Turicibacter and Megasphaera showed positive correlations with muscle parameters. In addition, enrichment of predicted microbial functions, such as amino acid metabolism, nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), was observed following supplementation with heat-treated LPMYO. Taken together, heat-treated LPMYO significantly improved muscle strength and muscle quality, and these muscle strength-enhancing effects may be associated with alterations in the gut microbiota.

papers.title: Microplastics as Microbiota Modulators: Rewiring the Gut Metabolism Immune Axis.
papers.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) have emerged as pervasive environmental contaminants with increasing relevance to human health. Beyond their role as inert particulate pollutants, accumulating evidence suggests that MPs may act as biologically active modulators of the gastrointestinal ecosystem. The gut represents a major interface for MP exposure, where ingested particles interact with intestinal epithelial cells, mucus layers, immune components, and resident microbial communities. This review summarizes current evidence on MPs' capacity to alter gut microbiota composition, impair intestinal barrier integrity, disrupt microbial metabolite production, and promote inflammatory and metabolic disturbances.Experimental studies indicate that MP exposure may reduce microbial diversity, shift the abundance of key bacterial taxa, impair tight junction proteins, and increase intestinal permeability. These changes may facilitate the translocation of bacterial products such as lipopolysaccharide, thereby activating inflammatory pathways including TLR4/NF-κB signaling. In parallel, MP-associated dysbiosis may alter short-chain fatty acids, bile acid metabolism, and tryptophan-derived metabolites, suggesting plausible biological pathways relevant to insulin resistance, hepatic lipid dysregulation, cardiometabolic risk, and gut-brain axis disruption. However, most available evidence is derived from animal and in vitro models, and causal relationships in humans remain insufficiently established. Major limitations include heterogeneous exposure protocols, non-standardized particle characterization, limited human longitudinal data, and difficulty separating particle-specific effects from those of associated chemical contaminants.Future studies integrating environmentally realistic exposure models, standardized microbiome analyses, multi-omics approaches, and human cohort designs are needed. Overall, the gut microbiota may represent a critical biological interface through which MPs interact with host physiology; however, further evidence is required before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding their role in human chronic disease susceptibility.

papers.title: L-Histidine alleviates tacrolimus-induced islet dysfunction via the gut-pancreas axis.
papers.abstract: Tacrolimus is widely used after organ transplantation but can impair pancreatic β-cell function and glucose homeostasis. Using rodent models, antibiotic-mediated microbiota depletion, fecal microbiota transplantation, 16S rRNA sequencing, metabolomic profiling, and MIN-6 cells, we examined whether microbiota-associated L-histidine contributes to β-cell protection. Tacrolimus altered gut microbial composition and increased histidine-associated microbial and metabolic signals. L-histidine supplementation improved glucose tolerance and insulin secretion, reduced β-cell apoptosis, and increased PI3K/Akt/mTOR/p70S6K signaling and PDX-1, NeuroD1, and MafA expression. Microbiota depletion attenuated several protective effects of L-histidine, supporting a contribution of the gut microbiota to this response. These findings connect a microbiota-associated amino acid with tacrolimus-related β-cell dysfunction and provide a framework for investigating microbiota-metabolite contributions to metabolic complications of immunosuppression.

papers.title: Tea Microbiomes and Metabolic Transformations From Fresh Leaf to Fermentation and Gut: Implications for Quality and Health.
papers.abstract: Microbiomes influence tea quality, safety, and health from production to consumption, yet most studies and reviews examine individual stages. This review uses the Tea Plant-Fermentation-Gut Continuum to assess cross-stage microbial and metabolic connectivity, not as an established transmission chain. It separates microbial origin and persistence from processing-associated chemical transformation and host responses. At the leaf-to-processing interface, phyllosphere and endophytic communities may contribute to the processing microbial pool, but taxonomic overlap does not demonstrate directional transmission, and strain-level persistence remains unproven. During processing, plant enzymes and microbial activities shape tea chemistry differently across tea types, affecting pigment and aroma development. At the processing-to-gut interface, current evidence mainly supports chemical and metabolic continuity: tea- and fermentation-derived compounds reach the gut and are metabolized by resident microbiota, whereas evidence that fermentation-associated microorganisms survive, persist, or colonize the gut remains insufficient. These metabolites are linked to FXR-FGF15, AMPK, and AhR signaling and to metabolic, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects, mostly in preclinical models; human evidence remains limited. Together, the evidence does not support an uninterrupted microbial transmission pathway across these stages. Key gaps remain in microbial origin, persistence, activity, causality, and host relevance. Shared taxa may reflect persistence, environmental acquisition, or compositional overlap rather than direct transmission; tea type, cultivar, processing, dose, and host microbiota limit generalization. Strain-resolved tracking, controlled experiments, functional omics, and metabolic tracing are needed to distinguish association from persistence, activity, and causal function. Addressing these gaps will support evidence-based tea processing, precision fermentation, and microbiome-informed nutrition.

papers.title: High Fat Diet Alters Gastrointestinal Function and Results in Reduced Enteric Neuron Density.
papers.abstract: Obese patients suffer from cardiovascular, metabolic and gastrointestinal disorders, including constipation, proposed to result from high fat diet (HFD)-induced enteric neuron loss.
